units.title: Why async
units.blurb: Waiting vs. working, Task as a promise of a result, and the big reveal: while I/O is in flight, no thread is needed.

lessons.title: Waiting is the enemy
lessons.sub: Why a window goes "Not Responding"

cards.title: A waiter by the stove
cards.body:
Picture a waiter who takes an order and then stands by the stove until the dish is ready. Every other table waits.

That is synchronous code: the thread waits for the network or the disk and does nothing else. A good waiter hands the order to the kitchen and goes to serve other tables. That is asynchrony.

cards.title: Why the window freezes
cards.body:
An app with a window (WPF, WinForms, Unity) has one main thread. It draws the UI and handles clicks.

If that thread is waiting for a server, the window stops responding: clicks pile up in the queue and nobody is there to handle them.

cards.task: Run the synchronous version to the end. On which tick is the user's click handled?
Now switch the handler to await and compare: when is the click handled?

cards.q: Why is the click handled almost at once with await?
options: While we wait for the network, the main thread is free to work through the message queue
cards.explain: await releases the thread while it waits. The network is no faster; the thread just isn't sitting idle.

cards.title: I/O vs. computation
cards.body:
There are two very different things you can wait for.

I/O: network, disk, database. The hardware does the work, and the thread just waits.
Computation (CPU): compression, physics, parsing. The processor itself does the work.

async/await is mainly about the first kind: how not to hold a thread while you wait.

cards.q: Which of these are I/O waits? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Compression and physics are CPU work. You can move them to another thread, but there is nothing to wait for.

cards.q: Does async/await make the server request itself faster?
options: No: the request takes just as long, but the thread isn't idle
Yes, if the server supports async
cards.explain: The win is that the thread does other work meanwhile: drawing the window or serving other clients.

cards.q: Where is a blocked main thread most noticeable?
options: In a windowed app or a game: the picture freezes
cards.explain: At 60 frames per second a game has just 16 ms per frame. Any wait on the main thread is a freeze.

lessons.title: Task: a promise of a result
lessons.sub: A claim ticket instead of the answer

cards.title: A Task is a claim ticket
cards.body:
A Task is an object meaning "work that will finish later". Think of a dry cleaner's ticket: your clothes aren't ready yet, but you hold a slip you'll trade for them later.

A Task<string> is a ticket you'll trade for a string.

cards.title: Get the ticket, collect later
cards.body: A task can be in progress, completed successfully, faulted with an error, or canceled.
cards.deep: TaskStatus: Created, WaitingForActivation, WaitingToRun, Running, WaitingForChildrenToComplete, RanToCompletion, Canceled, Faulted. Tasks from async methods and I/O are usually WaitingForActivation: they aren't "running" on any thread, and something outside will complete them.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: The same, with an int result

cards.q: A method returned Task<string>. Where is the string?
options: It may not exist yet: await hands it over when the task completes
cards.explain: A task is a promise. The result appears when the operation finishes.

cards.title: Task.Run is for computation
cards.body:
Task.Run(() => …) hands work to a thread-pool thread. Use it for heavy computation so the main thread stays free.

I/O doesn't need Task.Run: GetStringAsync already doesn't hold a thread.
cards.deep: Task.Run(async () => …) unwraps the inner task correctly. Task.Factory.StartNew with an async lambda returns Task<Task>, and await then waits only for the start. A classic mistake.

cards.q: You need to compress a large image without freezing the window. What do you do?
options: Call Compress(img) directly in the handler
cards.explain: Compression is CPU work. Task.Run moves it to the pool, and await brings the result back to the UI thread.

cards.q: Should you wrap http.GetStringAsync(url) in Task.Run?
options: No: the request doesn't hold a thread anyway; Task.Run just ties up a pool thread
Yes, or it will block the window
cards.explain: Async I/O already doesn't block. Task.Run on top is wasted work.

cards.q: How can a task end? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Those are the three final states. You can't pause a task.

cards.q: Get the result without blocking the thread
cards.code: string html = ___ http.GetStringAsync(url);
cards.explain: await "unwraps" a Task<string> into a string.

lessons.title: There is no thread
lessons.sub: Where is the thread during a request? Nowhere

cards.title: Where is the thread during a request?
cards.body:
Answer: nowhere. The request goes to the network card, and the OS waits for the reply on its own, with no thread. When data arrives, the OS tells .NET, and only then does a pool thread briefly pick up the continuation.

This is the famous "There is no thread", the title of an article by Stephen Cleary.
cards.deep: Under the hood are the OS mechanisms for async I/O: IOCP on Windows, epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS. A few .NET threads wait for notifications for all operations at once, not one thread per request.

cards.task: A console program awaits a reply. Step through the ticks and watch the "network" row: is any thread busy while we wait?

cards.q: 1,000 requests are awaiting replies. How many threads are busy waiting?
options: None: the OS waits, and threads only run continuations
cards.explain: A thread is needed only when there is code to run.

cards.task: Compare on the thread pool: add 16 requests with await and watch the thread count and wait time. Then try .Result if you like.

cards.q: Why can an async server handle more requests?
options: While requests wait on the database and network, threads serve other requests
cards.explain: Same number of threads, but none of them sits idle waiting.

cards.q: Does async speed up heavy computation?
options: Not by itself: computation still occupies a thread; you can only move it to the pool with Task.Run
cards.explain: async is about waiting. For parallel computation there are Parallel and PLINQ.

cards.q: Match them up
What happens on await http.GetStringAsync(url)?
items: The method sends the request
The thread goes back to other work
The OS waits for the reply with no thread
The reply arrives and the continuation is queued
A free thread runs the continuation
cards.explain: The thread is involved only at the start and at the end.

lessons.title: Final: why async
lessons.sub: Waiting, Task and the thread that isn't there

cards.task: Make the window handle the user's click by tick 2 at the latest.

cards.q: What does the thread do while await waits for the server?
options: Other work, or nothing if there is none
cards.explain: The OS waits, not the thread.

cards.q: Where does Task.Run make sense? Select all that apply.
options: Heavy computation started from the UI thread
Compressing a large file in memory
cards.explain: Async I/O doesn't need Task.Run.

cards.q: What has Task<int> LoadAsync() returned while the request is still running?
cards.explain: The result comes later; you can wait for the task with await.

cards.q: How is await different from .Result?
options: await doesn't block the thread, .Result does
cards.explain: Both wait for the result, but .Result holds the thread the whole time.

cards.q: The path of an async request
items: Send the request
Release the thread
The OS waits for the reply
The continuation is queued
A thread runs the continuation
cards.explain: A thread is needed at the start and at the end.

cards.q: A game makes a synchronous HTTP request on the main thread. What does the player see?
options: The picture freezes until the server replies
cards.explain: The main thread can't draw frames while it waits.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: No thread is busy while waiting

units.title: async and await in action
units.blurb: Your first async method, what to return, where exceptions go, WhenAll and WhenAny, and cancellation with CancellationToken.

lessons.title: Your first async method
lessons.sub: async, await and where a method pauses

cards.title: Two keywords
cards.body:
async on a method lets you use await inside it.

await takes a task. If the task isn't done yet, the method "pauses" and returns control to its caller. When the task finishes, the method picks up right where it left off.

cards.title: The start is synchronous
cards.body:
Until the first await that actually waits, an async method runs like any other: on the same thread, with no switching.

And if the task has already completed, await doesn't pause at all.

cards.q: What does the caller get when GetLengthAsync reaches await on an unfinished request?
cards.explain: The method returns a task right away, at its first real pause. The result comes later.

cards.q: On which line can the method pause?
cards.explain: A method can only pause at an await.

cards.q: return html.Length returns an int, but the method is declared Task<int>. Why is that allowed?
options: The compiler wraps the result in a task for you
An int automatically becomes a Task
cards.explain: In an async method, return sets the result of the future task.

cards.q: Make the method asynchronous
cards.explain: async goes in the declaration, await before the task.

cards.task: Same async code: run it in WPF, then in a console app. Who runs the continuation?

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: Until the first await, an async method runs synchronously
Awaiting an already completed task doesn't pause the method
An async method with no await inside runs synchronously
async by itself creates a new thread
cards.explain: async doesn't create threads or block. It's a way to cut a method into pieces around its waits.

cards.q: A method is marked async but has no await inside. What happens?
options: It runs synchronously, and the compiler warns you (CS1998)
cards.explain: No await means no pauses: the method runs to the end and returns an already completed task.

lessons.title: What to return
lessons.sub: Task, ValueTask and the dangerous async void

cards.title: Task, Task<T>, ValueTask<T>
cards.body:
Task: no result, but you can wait for it.
Task<T>: returns a T.
ValueTask<T>: the same, but with no allocation when the result is often ready at once (say, from a cache). You may await it only once.

cards.title: async void is for event handlers only
cards.body:
You can't await an async void: the caller never learns when the method finished. And you can't catch its exception from outside: it goes to the synchronization context and usually crashes the app.

Use async void only where an event dictates the signature: button.Click += async (s, e) => …

cards.q: Why is async void dangerous?
options: You can't await it, and a try around the call won't catch its exception
cards.explain: No task means nothing to wait on and nothing to carry the exception.

cards.q: Which line is a design mistake?
cards.explain: SaveAsync isn't an event handler. It should be async Task so callers can await it.

cards.q: When does ValueTask<T> beat Task<T>?
options: When the result is often ready at once and the method is called very often
When the method waits a long time on the network
cards.explain: You only save on the fast path with no waiting. If the method always waits, there is hardly any difference.

cards.q: What must you not do with a ValueTask? Select all that apply.
options: Await it from two places at once
cards.explain: Need more? Call .AsTask() and work with a regular task.
cards.deep: A ValueTask can wrap a reusable IValueTaskSource. After the first await, what it holds may already belong to another operation. Hence the strict rules.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: No allocation if ready at once

cards.q: Fix the signature
cards.explain: async Task is a method with no result that callers can await.

lessons.title: Exceptions
lessons.sub: await, .Result and AggregateException

cards.title: await throws like normal code
cards.body: If a task fails, await throws its exception: the very one thrown inside. A plain try/catch around the await catches it.

cards.title: .Result and .Wait() wrap it
cards.body:
If you wait synchronously with .Result or .Wait(), the exception arrives wrapped in an AggregateException, with the original inside, in InnerExceptions.

GetAwaiter().GetResult() throws the original exception, but it still blocks the thread.

cards.q: Will this catch block catch a network error?
cards.code:
try { var r = GetAsync().Result; }
catch (HttpRequestException) { … }
options: No: .Result throws AggregateException, with the HttpRequestException inside
cards.explain: One more reason not to block: deadlocks and awkward exceptions.

cards.task: Start three requests with Task.WhenAll and make two of them fail. How many exceptions does await throw, and how many are stored in the task?

cards.q: WhenAll, and A and C failed. What does await throw?
options: Only A's exception; all errors are in the WhenAll task's Exception.InnerExceptions
cards.explain: await unwraps and throws the first one. To see them all, keep the WhenAll task and check its Exception.

cards.title: Forgotten exceptions
cards.body:
If nobody awaits a task, nobody sees its exception. Since .NET 4.5 this doesn't crash the app; the error is simply lost (you can catch it with the TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException event).

That's why fire-and-forget hides errors.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: A WhenAll task keeps all errors in Exception.InnerExceptions
An exception from an unawaited task crashes the app at once
cards.explain: With await, try/catch works just as it does in synchronous code.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: The original, but the thread is blocked
An error from a task nobody awaited

lessons.title: Several tasks at once
lessons.sub: One by one, WhenAll and WhenAny

cards.title: One by one or together
cards.body:
You can await three independent requests one by one: await, await, await. The times add up.

Or you can start all three at once and wait for them together with Task.WhenAll. Then it takes as long as the slowest one.

cards.task: Three requests: 300, 500 and 200 ms. Get the total time down to 500 ms or less.

cards.q: How long does the sequential version take?
cards.explain: 300 + 500 + 200. Each request starts after the previous one ends.

cards.task: Go back to "one by one" and make the first request fail. What happened to the others?

cards.q: With sequential awaits, why did B and C never even start after A failed?
options: await A threw, and execution never reached the lines with B and C
cards.explain: An exception stops the method at the very first await.

cards.title: WhenAny: who's first
cards.body:
Task.WhenAny returns the first task to finish. Handy for "whoever answers fastest" and for timeouts.

WhenAny itself doesn't throw: check the winner or await it.

cards.q: You need data from the fastest of three mirrors. What do you use?
cards.explain: Cancel the other tasks with a token so they don't waste resources.

cards.q: Why do the requests still run one by one?
cards.explain: The await inside the loop waits for each request before starting the next. Add the tasks themselves to the list, without await.

cards.q: Start all the requests at once
cards.code:
var tasks = urls.Select(u => http.GetStringAsync(u));
string[] pages = await Task.___(tasks);
cards.explain: WhenAll returns an array of results in the same order.

lessons.title: Cancellation and timeouts
lessons.sub: CancellationToken: a polite request to stop

cards.title: Cancellation is a request
cards.body: Cancellation in .NET is cooperative: a CancellationTokenSource hands out a token, you pass it to methods, and they check it and stop on their own. You can't forcibly "kill" a task.

cards.q: The server didn't answer within 5 seconds. What happens?
options: The token is canceled, and GetStringAsync throws OperationCanceledException
cards.explain: HttpClient throws TaskCanceledException, which derives from OperationCanceledException.

cards.title: Your own code must listen too
cards.body: In a long loop, call token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested() and pass the token on to every async method. Otherwise cancellation gets stuck at your method.

cards.q: Where does cancellation get lost?
cards.explain: SaveAsync never got the token, so a save in progress won't be interrupted.

cards.q: How do you cancel a task that doesn't accept a token?
options: Not directly: you can only stop waiting for it, e.g. with WaitAsync(token)
cards.explain: WaitAsync (.NET 6+) stops the waiting, but the operation itself keeps running in the background.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: You can create a CancellationTokenSource with a timeout
Checking the token at the end of the method is enough
cards.explain: Code stops only where it checks the token.

cards.q: Pass cancellation along
cards.code: await SaveAsync(item, ___);
cards.explain: You pass the token itself to methods, not the source.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: Final: async in practice
lessons.sub: Types, exceptions, combinators and cancellation

cards.task: Load the three page sections as fast as you can.

cards.q: What does an async method return to its caller at its first real pause?
cards.explain: The result comes later, through that task.

cards.q: Which signature is bad?
cards.explain: UploadAsync isn't an event handler; it needs async Task.

cards.q: catch (HttpRequestException) around task.Result. Will it catch?
cards.explain: Waiting synchronously wraps exceptions.

cards.task: Show that WhenAll collects every error: make at least two tasks fail.

cards.q: Which are true about cancellation? Select all that apply.
options: You must pass it all the way down, into every async method
A long loop must check the token itself
A canceled task ends with OperationCanceledException
cards.explain: Nothing gets killed: code stops where it checks the token.

cards.q: Wait for the fastest mirror
cards.code:
Task<string> first = await Task.___(t1, t2, t3);
string page = await first;
cards.explain: WhenAny returns the winning task; one more await collects its result.

cards.q: When does ValueTask<T> pay off?
options: The method is called very often and the result is usually ready at once
The method always waits a long time on the network
cards.explain: The savings are on the fast path with no waiting.

cards.q: Match them up

units.title: Under the hood
units.blurb: What the compiler turns an async method into: the state machine, the awaiter, the fast path and ValueTask, ExecutionContext and AsyncLocal.

lessons.title: The state machine
lessons.sub: What the compiler turns await into

cards.title: await isn't magic, it's a switch
cards.body:
The compiler rewrites an async method into a struct: a state machine. Local variables become its fields, and the method body becomes a MoveNext function with the step number kept in a state field.

Every await is a spot where MoveNext can return and later come back.

cards.task: The responses are still on their way. Step through MoveNext and count the calls and pauses.

cards.q: How many times is MoveNext called for a method with two awaits if neither task is ready?
cards.explain: The first call is the start, then one more for each continuation after an await.

cards.q: Why isn't variable a lost between MoveNext calls?
options: It became a field of the state machine
cards.explain: The stack frame disappears between calls, but the struct's fields stay.

cards.task: Turn on "Results are ready" and walk through again.

cards.q: The results were already ready. How many pauses were there?
cards.explain: IsCompleted = true, so the method runs straight through in a single MoveNext call.

cards.title: On the stack, then on the heap
cards.body: In Release the state machine is a struct and lives on the stack as long as the method never pauses. On the first real pause it moves to the heap so it can outlive the method's return.
cards.deep: In .NET Core 2.1+ the state machine's "box" is the task itself: AsyncStateMachineBox derives from Task<T>, so a pause costs a single allocation. In Debug the state machine is a class so that Edit and Continue works.

cards.q: What does MoveNext do when it meets an incomplete awaiter?
items: Checks IsCompleted
Writes the step number to state
Subscribes MoveNext to completion via AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted
Returns control
cards.explain: That's how a method "pauses" without holding a thread.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Runs a piece of the method up to the next await
What we're waiting on right now

lessons.title: The awaiter pattern
lessons.sub: Why you can await almost anything

cards.title: await works with anything that has GetAwaiter
cards.body:
await x compiles to roughly this: get x.GetAwaiter(); if IsCompleted, call GetResult() right away; if not, subscribe with OnCompleted and return.

It's a pattern, not an interface: any type with the right methods works, even through an extension method.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: What to call when it's done
Take the result or the exception

cards.title: Your own awaitable in two lines
cards.body: Add a GetAwaiter extension method for TimeSpan, and you can await a span of time directly.

cards.q: Why did await TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1) compile?
options: TimeSpan got a GetAwaiter extension method, and that's all await needs
cards.explain: The compiler looks for GetAwaiter the same way foreach looks for GetEnumerator.

cards.q: Rebuild what await expands into
cards.explain: First the awaiter, then the readiness check.

cards.q: What does GetResult() do if the task failed?
options: Returns an AggregateException as a value
cards.explain: That's why await throws the original exception.

cards.q: What can you await? Select all that apply.
options: An int with no GetAwaiter of its own
cards.explain: All of them except int have a GetAwaiter.

cards.q: Why write await Task.Yield()?
options: To force the method to give up control and resume a bit later through the queue
To wait one frame in Unity
cards.explain: YieldAwaitable always reports IsCompleted = false, so the method is guaranteed to pause.

lessons.title: Fast path and allocations
lessons.sub: When await costs nothing

cards.title: Already done? No pause
cards.body: If the awaiter says IsCompleted = true right away, the method doesn't pause: no subscription, no thread switch, no extra objects. This is the fast path.

cards.task: Walk the fast path: the results are already ready.

cards.title: Where allocations hide
cards.body:
Every async method that pauses creates a heap object: the state machine together with its task.

Ready results can be returned with no allocation: Task.CompletedTask, ValueTask<T>. .NET caches some results itself, such as completed tasks holding true and false.

cards.q: A method reads a cache, and 99% of the time the data is there. What should it return?
options: ValueTask<T>: a cache hit allocates nothing
cards.explain: The fast path puts not a single object on the heap.

cards.q: Which line is the allocation-free fast path?
cards.explain: A ValueTask holding a ready value is a struct; the heap isn't touched.

cards.q: Which create no new heap objects? Select all that apply.
options: await on an already completed task
An async Task method that paused
cards.explain: Allocations show up where there is real waiting or new work.

cards.q: Can you await the same ValueTask twice?
options: No: the behavior is undefined; if you need more, call .AsTask() first
cards.explain: A ValueTask is single-use.

cards.title: Measure first
cards.body: If a method runs millions of times a second, its allocations show up in the profiler. If not, Task is simpler and safer. Optimize after you measure.
cards.deep: Since .NET 6 you can mark a method [AsyncMethodBuilder(typeof(PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder<>))], and then even a ValueTask method that pauses takes its objects from a pool. Turn it on selectively, after measuring.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A ready task with a result
No allocation on the fast path

lessons.title: Builder and ExecutionContext
lessons.sub: Who builds the task and what travels across await

cards.title: Who builds the task
cards.body: The state machine doesn't create the task itself. A builder does: AsyncTaskMethodBuilder<T>. It creates the Task, subscribes MoveNext to the awaiter and at the end calls SetResult or SetException.

cards.q: An exception is thrown inside an async method. What does the builder do?
options: Calls SetException: the task becomes Faulted, and await will throw the exception
cards.explain: The exception rides inside the task until someone awaits it.

cards.title: ExecutionContext travels with await
cards.body: Along with the continuation, .NET carries the ExecutionContext: the current culture, AsyncLocal<T> values and other "ambient" data. That's why AsyncLocal is still visible after await, even if a different thread runs the continuation.

cards.q: What does Log print after the await?
cards.explain: ExecutionContext carried the AsyncLocal value along with the continuation.

cards.q: How is ExecutionContext different from SynchronizationContext?
options: ExecutionContext is data that travels with code; SynchronizationContext is where execution resumes
cards.explain: ConfigureAwait(false) turns off the return to the SynchronizationContext, but ExecutionContext still flows.

cards.title: ThreadStatic vs. AsyncLocal
cards.body: A [ThreadStatic] field belongs to a thread: if another thread resumes the code after await, the value "vanishes". For per-request or per-operation data, use AsyncLocal.
cards.deep: If a called async method changes an AsyncLocal, the caller doesn't see the change after it returns: ExecutionContext is immutable and copied on write. Values flow down the call chain, not up.

cards.q: What flows across await with the ExecutionContext? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: ThreadStatic stays with its own thread.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Per-thread data, lost on a thread switch

lessons.title: Final: under the hood
lessons.sub: State machine, awaiter and contexts

cards.task: Walk the state machine in both modes: with waiting and with ready results.

cards.q: What does the state field hold?
options: The number of the await where the method stopped
cards.explain: The switch in MoveNext uses it to jump to the right spot.

cards.q: The awaiter pattern's methods
cards.explain: Subscribe to completion, then get the result.

cards.q: When does an async method allocate nothing on the heap?
cards.explain: The state machine struct stays on the stack.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: AsyncLocal survives a thread switch after await
The builder calls SetException on an exception
A ValueTask can be awaited many times
cards.explain: A ValueTask is single-use.

cards.q: Does ConfigureAwait(false) stop AsyncLocal from flowing?
options: No: it's about SynchronizationContext, while ExecutionContext always flows
cards.explain: These are two independent mechanisms.

cards.q: The life of an async method with one await
items: MoveNext #1 runs up to the await
The awaiter isn't ready: state is saved and the method returns
The task completes and MoveNext #2 is called
GetResult and the rest of the method
SetResult completes the task
cards.explain: Two MoveNext calls, one pause.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: The method body, cut at each await
The key that makes any type awaitable

units.title: Context and deadlock
units.blurb: SynchronizationContext, the classic .Result deadlock, ConfigureAwait(false), async all the way and thread-pool starvation.

lessons.title: SynchronizationContext
lessons.sub: Who runs the code after await

cards.title: Where code resumes after await
cards.body:
await remembers the current SynchronizationContext. In WPF and WinForms that means "the UI thread": the continuation is queued to the window and runs there, so you can touch controls.

A console app or ASP.NET Core has no context: any pool thread runs the continuation.

cards.task: Run the scenario in WPF, then switch to a console app and see who runs the continuations.

cards.q: Why can you write label.Text = … after await in WPF?
options: The continuation came back to the UI thread through the synchronization context
WPF lets you change controls from any thread
cards.explain: That's the main job of SynchronizationContext in windowed apps.

cards.q: Where is there a SynchronizationContext by default? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: A console app and ASP.NET Core have no context; the pool runs continuations.

cards.title: A context is a queue
cards.body:
The UI context is a queue: clicks, redraws, continuations after await. One thread works through it, one item at a time.

If that thread is busy or blocked, the queue stalls.

cards.q: The UI thread is busy with a long computation while a continuation waits in the queue. When does it run?
options: When the thread frees up and reaches it
cards.explain: The continuation waits its turn, just like clicks.

cards.title: When there is no context
cards.body: If no SynchronizationContext is set, await looks at the current TaskScheduler. By default that's the thread pool.
cards.deep: SynchronizationContext.Current and TaskScheduler.Current are checked at the moment of the await. You install your own context with SynchronizationContext.SetSynchronizationContext; that's how test frameworks and Unity run continuations on a single thread.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: Deadlock with .Result
lessons.sub: The classic UI deadlock

cards.title: A classic
cards.body:
The UI thread calls GetDataAsync().Result and blocks. Inside GetDataAsync, the continuation after await wants to return to the UI thread. But that thread is blocked, waiting for this very task.

Each waits for the other: a deadlock.

cards.task: Switch the handler to .Result and drive the program into a hang.

cards.q: What is the UI thread waiting for?
options: For the GetDataAsync task to complete
cards.explain: .Result blocks the thread until the task completes.

cards.q: And what is the task waiting for?
options: For the UI thread to run its continuation
cards.explain: The reply has already arrived. All the task needs is to run its continuation, which sits in the blocked thread's queue.

cards.task: Keep .Result, but move the code to a console app. Will it hang?

cards.q: Why doesn't .Result hang in a console app?
options: There's no context: a pool thread runs the continuation, and it's free
cards.explain: Without a context, the continuation doesn't need the blocked thread.

cards.title: Why it's still bad
cards.body:
In a console app or ASP.NET Core, .Result won't hang, but the thread still sits idle. Under load that's pool starvation (lesson 5).

Blocking on async code is bad everywhere.

cards.q: How a deadlock comes together
items: The UI thread calls GetDataAsync().Result and blocks
The request goes out to the network
The reply arrives and the continuation is queued to the UI thread
The UI thread can't run it: it's waiting for the task
Nobody ever gets what they're waiting for
cards.explain: The wait cycle: thread → task → thread.

cards.q: Where can this deadlock happen? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: It takes a single-threaded context. Old ASP.NET had one (AspNetSynchronizationContext); ASP.NET Core doesn't.

lessons.title: ConfigureAwait(false)
lessons.sub: Skipping the context, and when that's dangerous

cards.title: Don't go back to the context
cards.body:
ConfigureAwait(false) says: "the continuation doesn't have to run in the captured context". It goes to the pool instead.

That's right for library code that doesn't need the UI thread: fewer switches, and no deadlock if someone outside calls .Result.

cards.task: The code with .Result hangs. Fix it inside the library without touching the handler.

cards.q: What did ConfigureAwait(false) change?
options: A pool thread ran the continuation, and the task completed without the UI thread
cards.explain: The UI thread was still stuck on .Result, but the task no longer needed it.

cards.task: Now the method updates a window control after await. What happens with ConfigureAwait(false)?

cards.q: Why did it crash?
options: After ConfigureAwait(false) the code ran on a pool thread, and controls may only be touched from the UI thread
cards.explain: ConfigureAwait(false) belongs only where the code after await doesn't need the UI thread.

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
In libraries, use ConfigureAwait(false) on every await. In app code that touches the UI, leave it out.

But ConfigureAwait is a safety net, not a cure. The real cure for deadlock is not blocking at all: that's the next lesson.
cards.deep: .NET 8 added ConfigureAwaitOptions: for example, await task.ConfigureAwait(ConfigureAwaitOptions.SuppressThrowing) waits for the task without throwing. ASP.NET Core has no context, so ConfigureAwait(false) in app code changes nothing there.

cards.q: Where does ConfigureAwait(false) belong? Select all that apply.
options: In a button handler that then updates label.Text
In a Unity script that then moves a transform
cards.explain: Where the code after await touches the UI or the Unity API, you need the context.

cards.q: ConfigureAwait(false) is on the method's first await but not the second. What's the risk?
options: If the first task completed at once, the context never changed, and the second await captures the UI context again
cards.explain: An await that completes synchronously doesn't switch threads. That's why libraries put ConfigureAwait(false) on every await.

lessons.title: Async all the way
lessons.sub: How to really cure a deadlock

cards.title: Don't mix them
cards.body:
If the code inside is asynchronous, the code outside should await too, all the way up to the event handler or Main. That's async all the way.

Mixing them with .Result and .Wait() is called sync-over-async: it gives you both deadlocks and pool starvation.

cards.task: Fix the deadlock properly: no ConfigureAwait, just make the handler async.

cards.q: Why is await better than .Result in a handler?
options: The UI thread doesn't block: continuations and clicks keep running, so a deadlock is impossible
cards.explain: No blocked thread, no wait cycle.

cards.title: async Main and async handlers
cards.body: Since C# 7.1, Main can be async Task Main(). Event handlers are async void: the one sensible place for void. ASP.NET Core controllers return Task<IActionResult>.

cards.q: Where is the sync-over-async?
cards.explain: .Result holds a pool thread for the whole database query.

cards.q: Fix the controller
cards.explain: async in the declaration, await before the call.

cards.title: The reverse problem: async-over-sync
cards.body:
Wrapping a synchronous blocking call in Task.Run and naming the method …Async is a trick: a thread is still busy, just a different one.

Don't do this in a library: let the caller decide whether they need Task.Run.

cards.q: Which of these are sync-over-async? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Any synchronous wait on a task blocks the thread.

lessons.title: Thread-pool starvation
lessons.sub: The server doesn't crash, it crawls

cards.title: A server that crawls
cards.body:
ASP.NET Core has no context, so .Result won't hang. But every such request holds a pool thread while it waits for the database.

Under load the threads run out, the pool adds new ones slowly, and responses stretch to seconds while the CPU is nearly idle.

cards.task: Add 16 requests with .Result and start the clock. How many threads are stuck, and how does the pool grow?
Now the same 16 requests, but with await.

cards.q: What did the two exercises show?
options: Blocking requests tie up threads and bloat the pool; with await the same 4 threads cope
cards.explain: Waiting without a thread is the main win of async on a server.

cards.q: Under load, responses lag by seconds and the CPU is nearly idle. What do you suspect first?
cards.explain: An idle CPU with growing latency means the threads exist but are stuck.

cards.title: How to find it
cards.body: In dotnet-counters, watch the pool's queue length and thread count. A growing queue with low CPU usage is a sure sign.
cards.deep: dotnet-counters monitor --counters System.Runtime shows ThreadPool Queue Length and ThreadPool Thread Count. In a process dump (dotnet-dump) during starvation you'll see dozens or hundreds of threads whose stacks end in .Result or Wait.

cards.q: What can cause pool starvation? Select all that apply.
options: .Result and .Wait() on tasks that query a database
Thread.Sleep in code running on the pool
A synchronous read from a slow disk in every request
cards.explain: Anything that holds a pool thread without doing work.

cards.q: A quick "fix": ThreadPool.SetMinThreads(500, 500). What do you think?
options: It hides the symptom: threads still sit idle and eat memory; the cure is switching to await
cards.explain: Hundreds of waiting threads cost memory and context switches. The real cure is not blocking.

lessons.title: Final: context and deadlock
lessons.sub: Hang the program, then fix it three ways

cards.task: Drive the WPF app into a deadlock.
Fix it the right way: no ConfigureAwait, and stay in WPF.

cards.q: Which fix is a safety net rather than a cure?
cards.explain: The thread still blocks on .Result; the deadlock loop just never closes.

cards.q: Where do you need the captured context after await? Select all that apply.
options: A Unity script moves a transform
An ASP.NET Core controller reads the database
cards.explain: A library or a server doesn't need the UI thread.

cards.q: Which line can hang a WPF app?
cards.explain: .Result on the UI thread while SaveAsync awaits inside without ConfigureAwait(false).

cards.q: Why doesn't the same line hang an ASP.NET Core server?
options: There's no context, so the pool runs the continuation; but the thread still sits idle
cards.explain: Instead of a deadlock you get thread-pool starvation under load.

cards.q: The wait cycle in a deadlock
items: The UI thread waits for the task
The task waits for its continuation
The continuation waits for the UI thread
cards.explain: A closed loop.

cards.q: Match them up

units.title: Pitfalls and advanced topics
units.blurb: Fire-and-forget and async void, SemaphoreSlim instead of lock, TaskCompletionSource, IAsyncEnumerable and await using, Channel and Parallel.ForEachAsync.

lessons.title: Fire and forget
lessons.sub: Fire-and-forget, a missing await and async void

cards.title: Fire and forget
cards.body:
Calling an async method without await is called fire-and-forget. The compiler warns you (CS4014).

The danger: you won't know when it finished, and you won't see its error.

cards.q: Where is the missing await?
cards.explain: The saves were started but never awaited. Their errors will be lost.

cards.q: What ends up in the log?
options: "saved", even though the saves are still running or have already failed
The log entry appears after all the saves
cards.explain: Without await, the code doesn't wait for SaveAsync to finish.

cards.title: async void crashes the process
cards.body: An exception from async void goes to the SynchronizationContext where the method started. If there's no context (console, pool), it's thrown on the thread pool, and the process crashes.

cards.q: A console app calls an async void method that throws after an await. What happens?
options: The process crashes with an unhandled exception
A try around the call catches it
cards.explain: The call already returned, and the try around it finished long ago. Nobody is there to catch the exception.

cards.title: If you really must fire and forget
cards.body: Wrap the task so its error is sure to reach the log. On a server, use a BackgroundService or a queue for background work.

cards.q: What's wrong with fire-and-forget? Select all that apply.
options: You can't tell when the task finished
The task can outlive the object or request that started it
cards.explain: Speed is the same; it's all about control.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Can't be awaited; an exception crashes the process

lessons.title: lock and await
lessons.sub: An async lock: SemaphoreSlim

cards.title: No await inside lock
cards.body: The compiler won't allow it: error CS1996. A lock belongs to a thread, and after await the method may resume on another one. The lock would then be released by a thread that never took it.

cards.q: Why can't you await inside a lock?
options: lock is tied to a thread, and after await the method may resume on another thread
cards.explain: Monitor requires Exit to be called by the same thread that called Enter.

cards.title: SemaphoreSlim: an async lock
cards.body: SemaphoreSlim(1, 1) lets one caller in. Its WaitAsync waits without blocking the thread, and any thread can release it.

cards.q: Build an async lock
cards.explain: There's a Wait() too, but it blocks the thread.

cards.q: Why put Release in finally?
options: Otherwise an exception leaves the semaphore taken forever
cards.explain: A forgotten Release is a deadlock too, just a quiet one.

cards.q: What does new SemaphoreSlim(3, 3) mean?
options: Up to three callers can be inside at once
cards.explain: A counting semaphore limits concurrency, for example the number of simultaneous API requests.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: WaitAsync doesn't block the thread while waiting
SemaphoreSlim isn't tied to a thread
You can use lock around await
You can skip Release: the GC will release it
cards.explain: Nobody will release the semaphore for you.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A synchronous lock tied to a thread
An async lock with a counter

lessons.title: TaskCompletionSource
lessons.sub: Your own task, built from callbacks

cards.title: A task you complete yourself
cards.body: TaskCompletionSource<T> creates a Task<T> that you complete yourself: SetResult, SetException, SetCanceled. That's how you turn an old callback API into a clean await.

cards.q: What does tcs.TrySetResult(loc) do?
options: Completes tcs.Task with a result, and everyone awaiting it continues
Blocks the thread until there's a result
cards.explain: A task from TaskCompletionSource runs nothing by itself; something outside completes it.

cards.title: The catch: continuations run on your thread
cards.body:
By default, SetResult may run the waiters' continuations right inside itself: synchronously, on the thread that called it. If you're holding a lock at that moment, or you're inside another library's callback, you get surprise reentrancy and even deadlocks.

The RunContinuationsAsynchronously flag sends continuations to the pool instead.

cards.q: Why use RunContinuationsAsynchronously?
options: So the waiters' continuations don't run synchronously inside SetResult
So the task runs on another thread
cards.explain: SetResult returns right away, and the continuations run separately.

cards.q: Why TrySetResult rather than SetResult?
options: The event may fire twice: SetResult throws the second time, while TrySetResult returns false
cards.explain: Callbacks can repeat, but a task completes only once.

cards.q: Which line can leave the task hanging forever?
cards.explain: On an error, the task never completes. It needs tcs.TrySetException(e).

cards.q: How can you complete a TaskCompletionSource task? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Plus the Try versions of all three.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Complete it if not already completed

lessons.title: Async streams and await using
lessons.sub: await foreach, yield and DisposeAsync

cards.title: Data as it arrives
cards.body: A method with async and yield return returns an IAsyncEnumerable<T>: items arrive one at a time, and you can wait between them. You read it with await foreach.

cards.q: Why is IAsyncEnumerable<T> better than Task<List<T>>?
options: You can process the first items without waiting for all of them to load
cards.explain: You don't have to hold a million lines from a file in memory at once.

cards.q: Read an async sequence
cards.code:
___ ___ (var o in ReadOrdersAsync())
    Handle(o);
cards.explain: await foreach waits for each next item.

cards.title: Cancellation in an async stream
cards.body: The consumer passes a token with .WithCancellation(ct), and the generator method receives it in a parameter marked [EnumeratorCancellation].

cards.title: await using
cards.body: If cleaning up a resource is itself asynchronous (flushing a buffer to the network, closing a connection), the type implements IAsyncDisposable with a DisposeAsync() method. await using calls it and awaits it at the end of the block.
cards.code:
await using var conn = new SqlConnection(cs);
await conn.OpenAsync();

cards.q: How is await using different from using?
options: It calls DisposeAsync and awaits it without blocking the thread
cards.explain: A plain using would call the synchronous Dispose, which can block the thread.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: yield return in an async method gives you an IAsyncEnumerable
await foreach loads all items at once
cards.explain: Items arrive one at a time, and the finalizer is a completely different mechanism.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Get the token in a generator

lessons.title: Channel and Parallel.ForEachAsync
lessons.sub: Pipelines and limiting concurrency

cards.title: A pipeline: producer → consumer
cards.body:
A Channel<T> is an async queue: some code writes with WriteAsync, other code reads with ReadAllAsync.

A bounded channel (CreateBounded) makes a fast producer wait until the consumer catches up. This is backpressure.

cards.q: A channel with room for 100 items is full. What does WriteAsync do?
cards.explain: That's the default behavior (BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait). Dropping items happens only if you ask for it explicitly.

cards.q: Why bound a channel?
options: So a fast producer doesn't fill up memory when the consumer can't keep up
cards.explain: With no limit, the queue can grow until memory runs out.

cards.title: Parallel.ForEachAsync
cards.body: Since .NET 6 you can process a collection asynchronously with a concurrency limit. It won't fire off 10,000 requests at once.

cards.q: You need to download 10,000 files, at most 8 at a time. What do you pick?
cards.explain: WhenAll over 10,000 tasks will swamp the server, and a sequential loop will take forever.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: A Channel is an async queue between parts of a program
A bounded channel gives you backpressure
Parallel.ForEachAsync limits the number of concurrent operations
A Channel stores data on disk
cards.explain: WhenAll waits for everything you give it; limiting is up to you.

cards.q: Limit the concurrency
cards.explain: No more than 8 downloads at a time.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A queue with a limit and waiting
Read until the channel is closed
Process a collection with a limit

lessons.title: Final: pitfalls
lessons.sub: Find the bug in each snippet

cards.q: Where is the bug?
cards.explain: InsertAsync has no await: the commit runs before the inserts finish, and errors get lost.

cards.q: What won't compile?
cards.explain: CS1996: await inside lock isn't allowed. Use SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync.

cards.q: A TaskCompletionSource is completed from a library callback while the library holds its internal lock. What should you pass when creating it?
cards.explain: Otherwise the waiters' continuations run right under someone else's lock.

cards.q: Where is async void acceptable?
options: In a method that saves to the database
cards.explain: Everywhere except handlers, use async Task.

cards.q: How can you limit the number of concurrent requests? Select all that apply.
options: A bounded Channel with N consumers
cards.explain: WhenAll limits nothing.

cards.q: Clean up the connection asynchronously
cards.code: ___ using var conn = new SqlConnection(cs);
cards.explain: await using calls DisposeAsync.

cards.q: Why is IAsyncEnumerable good for reading a huge file?
options: Items are processed as they're read, without loading the whole file into memory
It reads the file on several threads
cards.explain: A stream of data instead of one giant list.

cards.q: Match them up

units.title: Platforms
units.blurb: ASP.NET Core, WPF and WinForms, Unity: Awaitable, coroutines, UniTask and cancellation tied to the object.

lessons.title: ASP.NET Core
lessons.sub: No context, but still no blocking

cards.title: No context on the server
cards.body:
ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext: any free pool thread runs the continuation after await. So the classic .Result deadlock doesn't happen here.

Old ASP.NET (Framework) did have a context, and .Result hung there just like in WPF.

cards.task: A request handler calls .Result. Run it to the end: will it hang?

cards.q: Why doesn't .Result hang here?
options: The continuation doesn't need a particular thread: any pool thread will run it
.Result works like await in ASP.NET Core
cards.explain: No context, so nothing is waiting on a main thread.

cards.title: But .Result still hurts
cards.body: While a request is stuck on .Result, its pool thread is busy doing nothing. A hundred such requests and the pool starves: new requests wait in the queue even though the CPU is free. It's the same pool starvation from unit 4.

cards.task: Rewrite the handler to use await and run it to the end.

cards.q: The server crawls under load, but the CPU is at 5%. The code has lots of .Result. What's going on?
options: Pool threads are blocked, and new requests can't get a thread
cards.explain: Classic pool starvation. The cure is await all along the chain.

cards.title: HttpContext lives only during the request
cards.body: Don't carry HttpContext or scoped services (like DbContext) into a background task: the request ends and they get disposed. Copy the data you need up front, and hand background work to a BackgroundService or a queue.

cards.q: Which line is dangerous?
cards.explain: The DbContext is disposed when the request ends, but the background task will still be using it.

cards.q: Which are true about ASP.NET Core? Select all that apply.
options: .Result doesn't cause the classic deadlock, but it blocks a pool thread
ConfigureAwait(false) in app code changes nothing
HttpContext is safe to use after the response
cards.explain: You must not use HttpContext after the request ends.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: WPF and WinForms
lessons.sub: The UI thread, Dispatcher and Task.Run

cards.title: One thread for every control
cards.body: A single UI thread draws the window and handles clicks. Controls may only be touched from that thread. await in a handler brings you back there on its own, which is why label.Text = ... works after await.

cards.task: After await, the handler writes to label.Text. Someone added ConfigureAwait(false), and everything broke. Fix it.

cards.q: Which exception do you get in WPF if you touch a control from another thread?
options: InvalidOperationException: "The calling thread cannot access this object because a different thread owns it"
cards.explain: WinForms throws a similar InvalidOperationException about a cross-thread operation.

cards.title: Getting back to the UI thread by hand
cards.body: If your code is already on another thread (a timer event, a library callback), ask the UI thread to do the work:

cards.title: Heavy computation goes to Task.Run
cards.body: await by itself doesn't move work off the UI thread: synchronous code before the first await runs right there. Hand heavy calculations to the pool with Task.Run, and show the result after await.

cards.q: A button handler has await CalculateAsync(), yet the window still freezes for 3 seconds. Why?
options: CalculateAsync computes synchronously until its first await, which means on the UI thread
cards.explain: async doesn't make code run in the background. Hand the calculation to Task.Run.

cards.q: Put what happens on a click in order
items: The handler starts on the UI thread
Task.Run hands the calculation to the pool
The UI thread is free and handles clicks
The calculation ends and the continuation is queued to the UI
The UI thread shows the result
cards.explain: While the pool computes, the window stays alive.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: await in a handler returns to the UI thread
Dispatcher.InvokeAsync runs code on the UI thread
Task.Run moves heavy calculation off the UI thread
A button handler must be async Task
cards.explain: The event sets the handler's signature, so async void is fine there.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: WPF: run on the UI thread
WinForms: run on the UI thread
Brings await back to the WPF UI thread

lessons.title: Unity
lessons.sub: The main thread, UnitySynchronizationContext and Awaitable

cards.title: Unity has a context too
cards.body: Almost the entire Unity API (transform, GameObject, components) works only from the main thread. Unity installs its own UnitySynchronizationContext: the continuation after await runs on the main thread, in the next frame.

cards.task: The script moves a transform after await. Run it as is.

cards.q: What error does Unity show?
options: UnityException: … can only be called from the main thread
cards.explain: ConfigureAwait(false) sent the continuation to the pool, and you can't touch a transform from there.

cards.task: Fix it: the continuation must return to the main thread.
Unity can hang too. Drive it into a deadlock.

cards.title: Awaitable: Unity's native async
cards.body: Since Unity 2023.1 (and in Unity 6) there's an Awaitable class: cheap waits with no extra allocations.
cards.deep: Awaitable objects come from a pool and go back to it when they complete. So you can't await the same Awaitable twice: the second await may get someone else's operation. If you need to await several times, wrap it in a Task.

cards.q: Compute in the background, then move the object
cards.explain: Without MainThreadAsync, the transform line will throw.

cards.q: Match them up
Can you await the same Awaitable twice?
options: No: the Awaitable goes back to the pool, and a second await is unpredictable
Yes, but only on the main thread
cards.explain: That's the price of zero allocations.

lessons.title: Coroutines, UniTask and cancellation
lessons.sub: What to pick in Unity and how not to outlive your object

cards.title: Coroutines: async before async
cards.body:
A coroutine is a method with IEnumerator and yield return. Unity advances it every frame. It lives as long as its MonoBehaviour: destroy the object, and the coroutine stops.

But a coroutine can't return a value, and it's bad at handling exceptions.

cards.title: async outlives the object
cards.body: An async method knows nothing about a GameObject's lifetime. Destroy the object, or exit Play Mode in the editor, and the method keeps running. A second later it touches a destroyed transform.

cards.q: The object is destroyed during await Awaitable.WaitForSecondsAsync(5). What happens to an async method with no cancellation token?
options: It keeps running and most likely fails when it touches the destroyed object
cards.explain: You have to cancel explicitly, with a token.

cards.title: destroyCancellationToken
cards.body: Since Unity 2022.2, every MonoBehaviour has a destroyCancellationToken that is canceled when the object is destroyed.

cards.q: Stop the patrol along with the object
cards.code: await Awaitable.WaitForSecondsAsync(2f, ___);
cards.explain: CancellationToken.None is never canceled.

cards.title: UniTask
cards.body: UniTask (Cysharp) is a popular library: an allocation-free struct task, waiting on Unity frames and events, and convenient cancellation. People used it before Awaitable existed, and still use it today for its rich API.

cards.q: Match each tool to what it is
pairs: IEnumerator and yield; dies with the object
Cancellation when the object is destroyed

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: A coroutine stops when its MonoBehaviour is destroyed
An async method stops by itself when the object is destroyed
A coroutine makes it easy to return a value
cards.explain: You have to cancel async yourself, and a coroutine doesn't return a value.

cards.q: You need to load data from a server and return the result to the game. What's more convenient?
options: async Awaitable<T> or UniTask<T> with a cancellation token
A coroutine with a global variable
cards.explain: Results, exceptions and cancellation come out of the box.

lessons.title: Final: platforms
lessons.sub: Server, window and game: one mechanism

cards.task: Find the platform where .Result doesn't hang.
A Unity script moves a transform after await. Make it all work without freezing frames.

cards.q: What do WPF and Unity have in common when it comes to async?
options: Both install a SynchronizationContext that returns the continuation to the main thread
cards.explain: That's also why .Result hangs in both.

cards.q: Where is ConfigureAwait(false) dangerous? Select all that apply.
options: In a WPF handler that then changes a control
In a Unity script that then touches a transform
cards.explain: In a library it helps, and in ASP.NET Core it changes nothing.

cards.q: Which line is missing cancellation?
cards.explain: Without destroyCancellationToken the wait won't be canceled, and the next line will touch a destroyed object.

cards.q: An ASP.NET Core server responds slower and slower under load, and the CPU is nearly idle. What do you suspect first?
options: Blocking .Result/.Wait() calls ate up the pool threads
cards.explain: Pool starvation. Use await all along the chain.

cards.q: Put the path of a continuation after await in WPF in order
items: await captured the UI context
The operation completed on a pool thread
The continuation was posted to the context (Post)
The UI thread took it from the message queue
The code after await ran on the UI thread
cards.explain: If the UI thread is blocked on .Result at that moment, step 4 never happens. That's the deadlock.

cards.q: Match each platform to its context
The main rule of the whole course?
options: Async all the way: don't block async code with .Result and .Wait()
cards.explain: Everything else is platform detail.

units.title: Tasks without await
units.blurb: ContinueWith and its traps, TaskScheduler and StartNew vs. Task.Run, child tasks, Parallel and PLINQ for CPU work, timers and who holds them, background threads, Register and linked tokens.

lessons.title: ContinueWith and its traps
lessons.sub: Continuations by hand: scheduler, exceptions, options and Unwrap

cards.title: A continuation by hand
cards.body:
Before await there was ContinueWith (.NET 4.0). It hangs a delegate on a task: when the antecedent task finishes — in any way: success, failure or cancellation — the delegate is queued to a scheduler.

ContinueWith itself immediately returns a new task — the continuation task. It completes once the delegate has run.
cards.deep:
A task has a field for continuations (m_continuationObject): it holds one object or a list. When the task completes, it walks that field. For ContinueWith the entry is a wrapper that queues a new Task to the scheduler.

await uses the same field but puts the state machine box there (as in the "Under the hood" unit). Hence the cost difference: each ContinueWith is a new task and a delegate (plus a closure), while an async method gets by with one box for the whole method.

cards.q: load completed with an error. What happens to the continuation load.ContinueWith(t => Log("done"))?
options: It runs: without options a continuation runs on any outcome
It does not run: the antecedent failure cancels the continuation
It throws AggregateException on the thread that called ContinueWith
It runs, but only after an explicit load.Wait()
cards.explain: By default (TaskContinuationOptions.None) a continuation does not care how the antecedent ended. Dealing with the error is its own job.

wrong.1: Only a continuation with OnlyOnRanToCompletion or NotOnFaulted behaves like that.

cards.title: Trap 1: TaskScheduler.Current
cards.body:
Where does the continuation run? ContinueWith without an explicit scheduler takes TaskScheduler.Current — the scheduler of the task whose code is running right now on this thread. Outside any task that is TaskScheduler.Default, i.e. the pool.

But inside a task started on a UI scheduler, Current is the UI scheduler. A "background" continuation or Task.Factory.StartNew from there silently moves to the UI thread. The window freezes even though no UI appears anywhere in the code.

The rule: always pass the scheduler explicitly to ContinueWith and StartNew. Analyzer CA2008 warns you if you forget.
cards.deep:
await works differently: it first looks at SynchronizationContext.Current, and only when there is no context does it look at TaskScheduler.Current, and only if that is not Default. That is why after await in UI code you come back to the UI thread through the context, not through a scheduler.

TaskScheduler.FromCurrentSynchronizationContext() bridges the two worlds: a scheduler that hands tasks to the current SynchronizationContext via Post.

cards.q: This code runs on the WPF UI thread. Which thread runs Heavy()?
options: The pool, if it has a free thread
cards.explain: The inner StartNew without a scheduler takes TaskScheduler.Current. The outer task runs on the UI scheduler, so Current is that scheduler, and Heavy() goes to the UI thread too. The fix is TaskScheduler.Default or Task.Run.

cards.title: Trap 2: exceptions
cards.body:
A continuation receives the antecedent as is. If it failed, t.Result throws AggregateException — like .Result in unit 2, only now inside the continuation.

That exception faults the continuation task. And usually nobody waits for it: the result of ContinueWith was thrown away. The outcome is silence: no error dialog, no log line. With await the exception would have reached the caller.

So check the outcome yourself in a continuation: t.IsFaulted, t.IsCanceled, t.Exception.
cards.deep:
What happens to an unobserved error: when the garbage collector collects a faulted task whose exception nobody read, the runtime raises TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException.

Then and now: in .NET 4.0 the process crashed after that. Since .NET 4.5 nothing happens by default (the ThrowUnobservedTaskExceptions setting could bring the crash back). In .NET Core and .NET 5+ there is only the event. So a lost error does not crash the app — it just vanishes, which is worse for debugging.

cards.q: LoadAsync failed. On which line is the exception thrown and lost without a trace?
cards.explain: t.Result on a faulted task throws AggregateException. It faults the continuation task, and nobody waits for it: Refresh did not even keep it. Render is never called, and nobody finds out.

cards.title: TaskContinuationOptions
cards.body:
Options refine when and how a continuation runs:

  • OnlyOnRanToCompletion, OnlyOnFaulted, OnlyOnCanceled, NotOnFaulted and so on — run only on the matching outcome;
  • ExecuteSynchronously — run right on the thread that completed the antecedent, without a queue. Only for short continuations;
  • RunContinuationsAsynchronously — do not run the continuation's own continuations synchronously;
  • LazyCancellation — when the token is cancelled, do not complete until the antecedent finishes.

The trap: if an OnlyOn… condition is not met, the continuation task becomes Canceled. Wait for it and you get TaskCanceledException.
cards.deep: ExecuteSynchronously is a request, not an order. If the antecedent has already completed when ContinueWith is called, the continuation runs right on the calling thread. A long chain of such continuations could dive deep into the stack, so the runtime watches the remaining stack and queues the continuation anyway when an overflow threatens. The scheduler may also refuse inlining.

cards.q: In the code above load completed successfully. What happens at await err?
cards.explain: The OnlyOnFaulted condition was not met, the delegate never ran, and err moved to Canceled. Awaiting a cancelled task throws TaskCanceledException.

wrong.2: err does not hang: it was moved to Canceled right away.
wrong.3: The delegate never ran — it never got to t.Exception.

cards.title: A task inside a task: Unwrap
cards.body:
If the continuation is itself asynchronous and returns a Task, ContinueWith returns Task<Task>. The outer task completes as soon as the lambda has returned the inner one — that is, at the first real await inside. You will not wait for the end of the work that way.

Unwrap() builds a proxy task: it completes together with the inner task — with its result, error or cancellation. Task.Factory.StartNew with an async lambda has the same story, mentioned in unit 1.
cards.deep:
Unwrap is an extension method from TaskExtensions, available for Task<Task> and Task<Task<T>>. It blocks nothing: the proxy subscribes to the outer task, then to the inner one. If the outer task failed or was cancelled, the proxy takes that outcome.

Task.Run with a Func<Task> does this unwrapping internally. await await nested also works, but reads worse.

cards.q: Run SaveAsync after load on the pool and get a task that completes together with the save
cards.explain: Default is the pool, no matter who called the code. Unwrap turns Task<Task> into a task that waits for the save itself, not just for its start.

cards.title: When ContinueWith still fits
cards.body:
await does all of that and more: it returns to the context, unwraps the exception and does not create a task per step. So await is the default.

ContinueWith remains for narrow cases:

  • hanging a cheap handler without making the method async — for example, logging the error of a task nobody awaits;
  • hot library code: the overload with state and a static lambda avoid a closure;
  • old code from the .NET 4.0 days.
cards.code:
static void LogIfFaulted(this Task task, ILogger log) =>
    task.ContinueWith(static (t, s) =>
            ((ILogger)s!).LogError(t.Exception, "Background task failed"),
        log, CancellationToken.None,
        TaskContinuationOptions.OnlyOnFaulted |
        TaskContinuationOptions.ExecuteSynchronously,
        TaskScheduler.Default);

cards.q: What is true about ContinueWith? Select all.
options: Without options a continuation runs on any outcome of the antecedent
Without an explicit scheduler it takes TaskScheduler.Current
An exception in the continuation reaches whoever called ContinueWith
A continuation with OnlyOnFaulted moves to Canceled after a success
Unwrap blocks the thread until the inner task ends
cards.explain: A continuation's exception stays in the continuation task — only whoever waits for it will see it. Unwrap blocks nothing; it builds a proxy task.

cards.q: Match the setting to what it does
pairs: Run only if the antecedent failed
Skip if the antecedent was cancelled
Run on the thread that completed the antecedent
Do not complete before the antecedent ends
The thread pool, wherever it is called from

lessons.title: The scheduler and StartNew
lessons.sub: TaskScheduler, TaskCreationOptions and child tasks

cards.title: Who runs a task: TaskScheduler
cards.body:
A task that has a delegate does not start itself. It is handed to a task scheduler (TaskScheduler), which decides where and when to run it:

  • TaskScheduler.Default — the thread pool;
  • FromCurrentSynchronizationContext() — into the current context, for example the UI thread;
  • ConcurrentExclusiveSchedulerPair — a ready-made pair for limits: "no more than N at once" and "strictly one at a time".

Tasks from async methods and TaskCompletionSource have no delegate: they are not run but completed from outside (as in unit 1). They need no scheduler.
cards.deep:
A custom scheduler derives from TaskScheduler and implements three methods: QueueTask (accept a task), TryExecuteTaskInline (may it run right now on this thread) and GetScheduledTasks (for the debugger).

Inlining happens, for example, on Wait() for a task that has not started yet: the waiting thread may run it itself instead of standing idle. One more detail: if there is no SynchronizationContext and TaskScheduler.Current is not Default, await resumes on that scheduler. Code under a ConcurrentExclusiveSchedulerPair stays under it after await.

cards.q: Which task never goes through a TaskScheduler at all?
options: A task returned by an async method
cards.explain: An async method's task is a promise without a delegate: the state machine builder completes it. The other three carry a delegate, and someone has to run it — that is exactly the scheduler's job.

cards.title: Task.Run is StartNew with the right settings
cards.body:
Task.Run arrived in .NET 4.5 as a shorthand for the most common case. It equals StartNew with three explicit decisions: no token, no child attachment, strictly the pool. And for an async lambda it also does Unwrap.

A "bare" Task.Factory.StartNew(work) differs in everything: scheduler Current (the trap from the last lesson), options None, no unwrapping.

You need StartNew when you need what it offers: a custom scheduler, LongRunning, a state object without a closure.

cards.q: What does this code print?
options: Does not compile: StartNew does not accept an async lambda
cards.explain: StartNew returned Task<Task>. The outer task completed when the lambda reached its first await and returned the inner task. await waited only for that. With Task.Run it would be about 1000.

cards.title: TaskCreationOptions
cards.body:
Creation options are hints for the scheduler and rules for task relationships:

  • LongRunning — work that takes a long time. The default scheduler gives it a dedicated thread instead of a pool thread: the pool keeps its worker and does not have to wait to inject new threads;
  • PreferFairness — into the pool's global queue rather than the current thread's local queue: closer to first come, first served;
  • AttachedToParent and DenyChildAttach — task relationships, more on them below;
  • HideScheduler — inside the task TaskScheduler.Current looks like Default;
  • RunContinuationsAsynchronously — as with TaskCompletionSource in unit 5.
cards.deep:
In the default scheduler LongRunning is literal: it creates new Thread(…) { IsBackground = true }, which runs one task and exits. Creating a thread means an OS object and a stack reservation, on the order of tens of microseconds or more. For short tasks the option hurts.

It is only a hint: a custom scheduler may ignore it. And with an async lambda the dedicated thread lives only until the first real pause.

cards.q: How long does the dedicated thread allocated for LongRunning live?
options: Until the first real pause at an await
As long as the loop spins, i.e. forever
Not at all: the option fails with an async lambda
Until the garbage collector collects the task
cards.explain: The delegate is an async lambda. At the first incomplete await it returns a task, and the thread is free — so it exits. The loop continues on pool threads. The dedicated thread was created for nothing. This loop does not need LongRunning: it does not hold a thread anyway.

cards.title: Child tasks: AttachedToParent
cards.body:
A task created inside a running task with AttachedToParent becomes its child:

  • the parent does not complete until all its children have. While it waits, its status is WaitingForChildrenToComplete;
  • children's exceptions end up in the parent's AggregateException.

Without the option a nested task is independent (detached): the parent knows nothing about it.

This is the "structured parallelism" model of .NET 4.0. New code does the same explicitly: collect the tasks and wait with WhenAll.
cards.deep: How it works: on creation a task checks which task is currently running on this thread. If AttachedToParent is set and that task has no DenyChildAttach, the parent's counter of unfinished children goes up. When the parent finishes its delegate, it decrements the counter for itself; each child decrements it on completion. Zero means the parent is complete.

cards.q: What does the code print?
cards.explain: The child is attached: Wait on the parent waits for it too. "parent" prints at once, "child" after 500 ms, and only then is the parent complete and "done" printed.

cards.title: Why Task.Run sets DenyChildAttach
cards.body:
Whether to attach is decided by the child, that is, by someone else's code. Imagine a library inside your Task.Run creates a task with AttachedToParent. Your task suddenly waits for foreign work and receives foreign exceptions — and you never asked for that.

DenyChildAttach on the parent silently cancels such requests: the child becomes an ordinary independent task, without any error. Task.Run always sets it.

cards.q: In the code from the previous exercise the outer StartNew was replaced with Task.Run. What changes?
options: done prints before child: the child does not attach
Nothing: the child's option beats the parent's settings
child never prints: the child task gets cancelled
cards.explain: Task.Run sets DenyChildAttach, and the child's AttachedToParent is silently ignored. Wait covers only the parent body: "parent", "done", and "child" after 500 ms if the process is still alive.

cards.q: Hardware polling is a blocking loop that runs for hours. Give it a dedicated thread without touching the pool, strictly through the standard scheduler
cards.code:
Task.Factory.StartNew(PollHardware,
    CancellationToken.None,
    TaskCreationOptions.___ | TaskCreationOptions.DenyChildAttach,
    TaskScheduler.___);
cards.explain: LongRunning with the default scheduler gives a dedicated thread. Default so as not to depend on which task the code is called from.

cards.q: What is true? Select all.
options: Task.Factory.StartNew without a scheduler takes TaskScheduler.Current
Task.Run unwraps the Task<Task> from an async lambda
LongRunning guarantees a dedicated thread with any scheduler
PreferFairness makes a task run faster
cards.explain: LongRunning is a hint: only the default scheduler turns it into a dedicated thread. PreferFairness changes the queue, not the speed.

cards.q: Match the option to its effect
pairs: A dedicated thread instead of the pool
The global queue instead of the local one
The parent waits for this child

lessons.title: Parallel and PLINQ
lessons.sub: Every core on one job — and when it does not pay off

cards.title: Data parallelism
cards.body:
async is about waiting. This is something else: computation. The same operation over many elements, spread across all cores. For that there are Parallel.For, Parallel.ForEach, Parallel.Invoke and PLINQ.

The key fact about Parallel.For: it is synchronous. The calling thread blocks until all iterations finish, and it takes iterations itself too. Pool threads pick up the rest.

This is a tool for CPU work. For I/O there is Parallel.ForEachAsync from unit 5.
cards.deep:
Inside, Parallel creates a "replicating" task: the calling thread runs it itself, and its copies go to the pool. Each copy grabs ranges of indices, and the ranges grow as work proceeds — this balances the load even when iterations differ in length.

MaxDegreeOfParallelism defaults to −1, meaning no limit: the pool decides how many workers to give. If the loop body blocks, the pool injects threads, and the loop happily takes those too. So a blocking body in Parallel is a road to the pool starvation from unit 4.

cards.q: A WPF button handler calls Parallel.For with 3 seconds of heavy work. What happens to the window?
options: It freezes: Parallel.For is synchronous and occupies the calling thread
It does not freeze: all iterations go to the pool
It throws InvalidOperationException: not allowed from the UI thread
It freezes only on a single-core machine
cards.explain: The UI thread waits for the loop to end and computes iterations itself. The fix: await Task.Run(() => Parallel.For(…)) — then a pool thread does the waiting and the UI thread is free.

cards.title: Shared data: races and local totals
cards.body:
Iterations run at the same time. Each writing its own cell is fine. Changing a shared variable is a race, like count++ from two threads in ".NET under the hood". And a lock in every iteration lines the threads up in a queue, and the parallelism is gone.

The pattern: each worker keeps its own local total and merges it into the shared one once at the end. There is an overload with localInit and localFinally for that.
cards.code:
long total = 0;
Parallel.For(0, data.Length,
    () => 0L,                                    // localInit: a total per worker
    (i, state, local) => local + data[i],        // body: only the local sum
    local => Interlocked.Add(ref total, local)); // localFinally: merge once

cards.q: Which line loses increments?
cards.explain: count++ is a read, an add and a write. Two threads read the same value, both write +1, and one increment is lost. Use Interlocked.Increment or local totals.

cards.title: Stopping, exceptions, Invoke
cards.body:
• ParallelLoopState.Stop() — stop as soon as possible;
  • ParallelLoopState.Break() — do not start iterations with higher indices, but finish all lower ones. Used to find the first match;
  • ParallelOptions: MaxDegreeOfParallelism and CancellationToken (on cancellation — OperationCanceledException);
  • an exception in an iteration: no new iterations start, running ones finish, and all errors arrive as one AggregateException.

Parallel.Invoke runs several different actions and returns when all are done.

cards.q: You are looking for the element with the lowest index that matches a condition. What do you call in the iteration that found one?
cards.explain: Break guarantees that all iterations with lower indices will run: if one of them matches, you will not miss it. The lowest index Break was called from is in ParallelLoopResult.LowestBreakIteration.

wrong.1: Stop may leave lower-index iterations unexecuted — the element you found is not necessarily the first.
wrong.2: return ends only the current iteration; the loop goes on.

cards.title: PLINQ: AsParallel
cards.body:
PLINQ is parallel LINQ to Objects. AsParallel() turns a sequence into a ParallelQuery<T>, and the operators after it run on several threads.

  • The query is lazy, like regular LINQ: the work starts on foreach or ToList.
  • Order is not preserved. AsOrdered() restores the source order at the cost of buffering.
  • WithDegreeOfParallelism(n) — how many workers (by default as many as cores), WithCancellation(ct) — cancellation.
  • ForAll(action) — process results right on the worker threads, without merging them into one thread.
cards.code:
var hits = files
    .AsParallel()
    .WithDegreeOfParallelism(4)
    .Where(f => Hash(f) == target)   // computed on 4 threads
    .ToList();                       // results are merged, any order
cards.deep:
PLINQ analyzes the shape of the query and, for some combinations of operators, decides to run it sequentially if it thinks parallelism will not pay off. WithExecutionMode(ParallelExecutionMode.ForceParallelism) forces parallel execution.

WithMergeOptions controls how results are handed to the consumer: NotBuffered — one at a time right away, FullyBuffered — all at once at the end, AutoBuffered — in chunks (the default).

cards.q: What is guaranteed about the order of elements in r?
cards.code:
int[] r = Enumerable.Range(1, 8)
    .AsParallel()
    .Select(x => x * 10)
    .ToArray();
options: Nothing: without AsOrdered the order can be anything
Source order: ToArray restores it by itself
