Source order: Range knows its indices in advance
Reverse: the last thread writes first
cards.explain: Without AsOrdered PLINQ promises no order, even if on a small example it often matches the source. If you need order, use AsParallel().AsOrdered().

cards.title: When parallelism loses
cards.body:
• A cheap body. Partitioning, delegate calls and merging cost more than x * 2. A thousand such iterations are faster sequentially.
  • Shared state under a lock. Threads queue up behind the lock.
  • Memory-bound work. A simple pass over a huge array is limited by RAM bandwidth, not by the number of cores.
  • False sharing. Threads write to neighboring cells of one cache line and bounce it between cores (cache lines are covered in the "Memory in .NET" course).
  • I/O inside. Pool threads just sit and wait. Here you need Parallel.ForEachAsync or WhenAll.

Measurement decides, not intuition: BenchmarkDotNet on real data.
cards.deep:
For a cheap body, slice the range coarsely: Partitioner.Create(0, n) hands out "from — to" pairs, and inside each one runs a plain for. One delegate call per chunk instead of per element:

Parallel.ForEach(Partitioner.Create(0, n), r => { for (int i = r.Item1; i < r.Item2; i++) a[i] *= 2; });

cards.q: Why does "all downloaded" print before everything is downloaded? Find the line.
cards.explain: Parallel.ForEach takes an Action<T>, and the async lambda becomes async void. Each iteration returns at its first await, and the loop considers it done. Errors from async void will also crash the process. For I/O, use await Parallel.ForEachAsync.

cards.q: Where will Parallel.For or PLINQ most likely speed things up? Select all.
options: Computing SHA-256 for 10,000 large in-memory buffers
Multiplying each element of a 1000-int array by 2
Rendering a 4K frame pixel by pixel with a heavy formula on the CPU
Adding to a shared counter under a lock in every iteration
cards.explain: Heavy independent CPU work speeds up. 1000 multiplications are cheaper than the overhead, HTTP is waiting, and a shared lock lines threads up in a queue.

cards.q: Spread heavy log parsing over 4 threads with PLINQ
cards.code:
var errors = lines
    .___()
    .___(4)
    .Where(l => Parse(l).IsError)
    .ToList();
cards.explain: AsParallel turns PLINQ on, WithDegreeOfParallelism limits the number of workers. MaxDegreeOfParallelism is a ParallelOptions property for the Parallel class, not a PLINQ operator.

cards.q: Match the tool to the job
pairs: An index loop with CPU work
Keep the source order in PLINQ

lessons.title: Timers, threads and cancellation
lessons.sub: Who holds a timer, who holds the process, and how to link cancellations

cards.title: Timers: who calls you and where
cards.body:
• System.Threading.Timer — calls the callback on a pool thread every period. If the callback takes longer than the period, the next one starts without waiting — callbacks overlap on different threads. Change reschedules, Timeout.Infinite turns it off.
  • System.Timers.Timer — a wrapper with an Elapsed event and AutoReset, also on the pool.
  • UI timers (DispatcherTimer, System.Windows.Forms.Timer) — the tick goes through the message queue on the UI thread. No overlap, but a long handler freezes the window.
cards.deep:
An exception from a System.Threading.Timer callback is an unhandled exception on a pool thread: the process crashes. System.Timers.Timer, per its documentation, swallows exceptions from Elapsed handlers — the error simply vanishes.

The runtime keeps timers in its own queues; a service thread tracks when they fire, and the callbacks go to the pool. Since .NET 8 there is TimeProvider: TimeProvider.System.CreateTimer(…) in code and a fake provider in tests — time can be "advanced" without real waiting.

cards.q: A System.Threading.Timer has a 1 s period, and the callback runs for 3 s. What happens?
options: Callbacks overlap: a second later the next one starts on another thread
The timer waits for the callback to end and shifts the next tick
Extra ticks are dropped; there is always one callback
The timer throws an overload exception
cards.explain: The timer does not know whether you are done. About three callbacks will run at once, and shared data in them must be protected. If you do not want overlap, re-arm the timer with Change at the end of the callback or use PeriodicTimer.

cards.title: Who holds the timer
cards.body:
A running timer is registered in a runtime queue, but the queue holds an internal part, not your Timer object. If nobody keeps a reference to the Timer, the garbage collector may collect it — the finalizer stops the timer, and the ticks silently end. The documentation says it plainly: keep a reference to the timer for as long as you need it.

The nasty part is that the bug comes and goes. If the timer is a local variable of a long method, in a Debug build the JIT extends its lifetime to the end of the method, and everything works. In Release the variable is dead right after its last use.

The flip side: while a timer is active, the queue holds the callback and everything it captured. A timer in a field of the object whose method it calls holds that object in a circle: queue → callback → object → timer. Such a timer will never be collected on its own — stop it with Dispose.
cards.deep: In .NET Core a timer is split into three objects: Timer → TimerHolder (with a finalizer) → TimerQueueTimer. The queue references only the last one. So an abandoned Timer and its holder become garbage, and the holder's finalizer closes the TimerQueueTimer — otherwise a forgotten timer would tick forever.

cards.q: What happens to the ticks?
options: They go on forever: the timer sits in a runtime queue
They never start: a timer needs a dedicated thread
After each collection they come twice as often
cards.explain: After StartTicking returns, not a single reference to the Timer is left. A collection will collect it, and the finalizer stops the timer. The runtime queue holds only the internal part, not your object. The fix: keep the timer in a field and release it with Dispose.

cards.title: PeriodicTimer: a timer for async
cards.body:
PeriodicTimer (.NET 6) works without callbacks — as a loop with await WaitForNextTickAsync:

  • ticks do not overlap: the next iteration starts only when you come back to wait;
  • missed ticks do not pile up: if the work took three periods, at most one tick is pending, and the next wait completes immediately;
  • stopping — Dispose (the wait returns false) or a token (throws OperationCanceledException);
  • only one consumer may wait at a time.

.NET 8 added a Period property you can change on the fly, and a constructor that takes a TimeProvider.
cards.deep: Inside it is the same TimerQueueTimer. WaitForNextTickAsync returns a ValueTask<bool> over a reusable IValueTaskSource, so a tick creates no new task. That is also where the "one waiter" limit comes from: the timer has a single source.

cards.q: Sync once a minute without overlap
cards.explain: The loop sets the pace itself: while SyncAsync is running, a new tick will not start a second instance.

cards.title: Background and foreground threads
cards.body:
A process lives as long as at least one foreground thread is alive. Main has returned, but a new Thread(…) is still running — the process waits for it.

Background threads (IsBackground = true) do not hold the process. When the last foreground thread ends, the runtime stops background threads where they are: no exception, and finally does not run.

  • Background: all pool threads — so Task.Run, timer callbacks, continuations after await; the LongRunning thread.
  • Foreground: the main thread and new Thread by default.
cards.deep:
For a clean shutdown, do not rely on a thread — give it a signal: in the .NET host that is BackgroundService and its stoppingToken, for the process — the AppDomain.ProcessExit event.

Then and now: .NET Framework had Thread.Abort — "kill" a thread with an exception. In .NET Core and .NET 5+ it throws PlatformNotSupportedException. Foreign code can only be stopped cooperatively.

cards.q: A console app. Will done.txt appear?
options: No: the pool thread is background, the process exits first
Yes: the process waits for all unfinished tasks
Yes: Task.Run creates a foreground thread
cards.explain: Main has returned, no foreground threads are left — the process exits, and the task is cut off during Sleep. You need to wait for it: await Task.Run(…) in an async Main.

cards.title: Register: what to do at the moment of cancellation
cards.body:
token.Register(callback) subscribes a callback to cancellation. That is how you connect cancellation to APIs without tokens: close a socket, cancel a TaskCompletionSource.

  • The callback runs synchronously on the thread that called Cancel() — right inside Cancel.
  • If the token is already cancelled, the callback runs immediately, inside Register itself.
  • Cancel collects callback exceptions into an AggregateException after all of them have run.
  • Register returns a CancellationTokenRegistration. Do not release it, and the callback and everything it captured live as long as the token source.
cards.deep:
Disposing a registration waits if the callback is running right now on another thread: afterwards the callback is guaranteed to have finished. Hold a lock the callback needs and you get a deadlock. Unregister() (.NET Core 3.0) removes the subscription without waiting.

Register(cb, useSynchronizationContext: true) posts the callback to the context captured at registration. CancelAsync() (.NET 8) runs the callbacks off your thread and returns a task.

cards.q: What does the code print?
cards.explain: The token is already cancelled, so Register runs the callback immediately and synchronously, before it returns. A late subscriber does not miss the cancellation.

cards.title: Linked tokens and CancelAfter
cards.body:
Often there are two reasons to cancel: the caller changed their mind, and your own timeout expired.

  • CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(a, b) — a new source that is cancelled when any parent is (or by itself);
  • CancelAfter(time) — cancel on an internal timer. Calling it again resets the deadline;
  • a linked source subscribes to its parents via Register, so it must be disposed. Otherwise a long-lived parent accumulates subscriptions.

Check who cancelled in a when filter.
cards.deep:
How a task becomes Canceled rather than Faulted. For an async method, any OperationCanceledException that escapes makes the task Canceled. For Task.Run(work, ct) — only if the exception carries that same ct and it is cancelled; otherwise Faulted. That is why ThrowIfCancellationRequested beats a manual throw: the exception carries the right token from the start.

TryReset() (.NET 6) returns a non-cancelled source to its initial state — for pooling. Since .NET 8 the constructor accepts a TimeProvider, and a timeout can be tested without real waiting.

cards.q: The service runs for weeks, and memory slowly grows. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: The linked source subscribed to appStopping, which lives for the whole lifetime of the service. Without Dispose each subscription stays in its list together with the source. You need using var cts.

cards.q: Match the tool to what it gives you
pairs: A callback at the moment of cancellation
Cancellation for any of several reasons
The thread does not hold the process

lessons.title: Final: tasks without await
lessons.sub: ContinueWith, schedulers, Parallel, timers and cancellation

cards.q: A WPF button handler, not inside any task. Where does Heavy() run?
options: On the pool: outside a task TaskScheduler.Current is Default
On the UI thread: StartNew takes the current SynchronizationContext
On the UI thread: StartNew without a scheduler takes Current
On a new dedicated thread: that is how StartNew works by default
cards.explain: Current is the scheduler of the running task, not the thread's context. A button handler is not a task, so Current is Default. The trap fires only when the code is already inside a task on a UI scheduler. It is safer not to guess and to write Task.Run.

cards.q: Which line throws TaskCanceledException whatever the outcome of LoadAsync?
cards.explain: Of the two continuations one is always skipped and moves to Canceled: on success it is log, on failure it is show. WhenAll with a cancelled task is cancelled too, and await throws TaskCanceledException.

cards.q: How does Task.Run(work) differ from Task.Factory.StartNew(work)? Select all.
options: Task.Run unwraps the Task<Task> from an async lambda
Task.Run allocates a dedicated thread for long work
Task.Run picks up the caller's cancellation token by itself
cards.explain: Task.Run = StartNew with DenyChildAttach, TaskScheduler.Default and Unwrap for async lambdas. Only LongRunning gives a dedicated thread, and Task.Run uses only a token passed to it explicitly.

cards.q: Inside Task.Run a library creates a task with AttachedToParent and throws from it. What does await on your task see?
options: Nothing: the child did not attach, its error stays in its own task
An AggregateException with the child's error
Your task waits for the child and completes together with it
cards.explain: DenyChildAttach on the Task.Run task silently turns the child into an independent task. No waiting, no foreign exceptions. The child's error is the concern of whoever created it.

cards.q: You need a report in the source row order, but the heavy formula should run on all cores. What do you add?
cards.explain: AsOrdered makes PLINQ return results in the source order while computing them in parallel. WithDegreeOfParallelism(1) kills the parallelism, and OrderBy sorts by value, not by position.

cards.q: A PeriodicTimer has a 5 s period, and the work in the loop takes 8 s. How do the runs go?
options: Back to back: one missed tick is pending, extra ones do not pile up
Overlapping: a new instance starts every 5 s
Every 10 s: a missed tick postpones the next one
Missed ticks accumulate, and the loop catches up on them
cards.explain: While the work runs, the timer remembers at most one tick. The next wait completes immediately, and the work takes 8 s again. No overlap: a new iteration does not start until you return to WaitForNextTickAsync.

cards.q: A background thread (IsBackground = true) is writing a file in try/finally when Main ends. What about finally?
options: It does not run: the runtime stops background threads without an exception
It runs: on exit a ThreadAbortException is raised in the thread
The process waits until the background thread finishes the file
cards.explain: Background threads do not hold the process. When the last foreground thread ends, they are cut off where they are, and finally does not run. For a clean exit — a cancellation token and waiting for the work.

cards.q: Cancel the request if the caller cancels or 10 seconds pass, and leave no subscription on someone else's token
cards.explain: The linked source is cancelled for either reason, CancelAfter adds the timeout, and using removes the subscription on ct when the method ends.

cards.q: Match them and test yourself on the whole unit
pairs: A task that waits for the inner task
A dedicated thread for blocking work
Finish the iterations with lower indices
A continuation without the scheduler queue
A callback on the thread that called Cancel

units.title: Synchronization in depth
units.blurb: The memory model and volatile, Interlocked and the CAS loop, spinning vs kernel objects, Monitor and the Lock type, Lazy<T> and concurrent collections. The course final.

lessons.title: The memory model and volatile
lessons.sub: Which reorderings are possible, x64 vs ARM64, Volatile.Read/Write

cards.title: Order in code is not order in memory
cards.body:
In the threads unit the race was easy to picture: two threads take turns doing the steps of count++. There is a subtler problem. Even without shared counters, another thread can see your writes in a different order than you wrote them.

Three parties change the order:

  • the C# compiler — almost never, it does little optimization;
  • the JIT — merges reads, keeps a field in a register, reorders independent operations;
  • the CPU — executes instructions out of order and queues writes in a store buffer before they reach the cache.

All three promise one thing: within one thread the result is as if the code ran strictly in order. They promise nothing about other threads — except what the rules of the memory model guarantee.

cards.title: The loop that never stops
cards.body:
A classic. One thread spins until a flag is raised, another thread raises it.

The JIT sees that nothing inside the loop changes _stop. So it may read it once before the loop and keep testing a register. For a single thread that is a fair optimization. For two threads it is an endless loop: the other thread did write to memory, but this thread never looks at memory again.
cards.deep:
In a Debug build and at tier 0 of tiered compilation the JIT barely optimizes, and the code "works". Once a hot method is recompiled at tier 1 (or replaced mid-loop through OSR, on-stack replacement), the read is hoisted out of the loop and the program hangs. That is why the bug shows up "only in Release and only sometimes".

The memory model spec in the dotnet/runtime repository allows this explicitly: adjacent ordinary reads of the same location can be coalesced into one.

cards.q: Release build, Run() spins in one thread, a second later another thread calls Stop(). What happens?
options: It may hang forever: the read of _stop was hoisted out of the loop
It always prints "done": a bool is written atomically
It prints "done", but only after a scheduler quantum
cards.explain: Atomicity is not the issue: writing a bool is indeed indivisible. The problem is visibility — the Run thread no longer reads the field from memory. The fix is Volatile.Read(ref _stop) or volatile on the field.

wrong.1: Atomic means "you will not read half a value". It does not promise the read happens at all.

cards.title: Four reorderings: x64 vs ARM64
cards.body:
Take two operations on different memory locations. The pairs are: read→read, read→write, write→write, write→read. Which of them the CPU can "swap" as seen from another core depends on the architecture.

  • x64 has a strong model (TSO). Only one reordering is visible: a write followed by a read of another location. The write is still sitting in the buffer while the read already went to the cache.
  • ARM64 has a weak model. All four are possible. That is Apple M-series, Graviton, Ampere, phones.

Hence a nasty class of bugs: code ran for years on x64 servers, and after moving to ARM64 it starts seeing "impossible" states once a day. And the JIT may reorder on its own, on any architecture.
cards.deep: TSO is total store order: all cores see writes in a single common order, and a core reads its own not-yet-flushed writes from the buffer (store forwarding). That is why write→read is the only hardware reordering on x64, and only a full fence fixes it: the mfence instruction or any lock-prefixed instruction.

cards.q: Which reordering of operations on different locations can an x64 CPU show to another core?
options: A write, then a read: the read overtakes the write
A read, then a write: the write overtakes the read
cards.explain: The write waits in the store buffer while the next read of another location has already executed. x64 does not do the other three — ARM64 does all four.

cards.title: Publishing through a flag
cards.body:
Thread A prepares data and raises a flag. Thread B sees the flag and reads the data. On ARM64, B can see _ready == true but a stale _data == 0: A's writes became visible in reverse order, or B's reads executed in reverse order.

Two promises are needed:

  • the flag write is a release: everything A did before it becomes visible no later than the flag;
  • the flag read is an acquire: everything B does after it will not run earlier.

That is exactly Volatile.Write and Volatile.Read.

cards.q: Fix the loop from the start of the lesson without changing the field declaration
cards.explain: Volatile.Read cannot be merged with neighboring reads or hoisted out of the loop — the thread looks at memory every time. Volatile.Write makes the write a release. Exchange and MemoryBarrier would also work, but they are full fences — more expensive and not needed here.

cards.title: The volatile keyword and what it does not give you
cards.body:
volatile on a field turns every read into Volatile.Read and every write into Volatile.Write. Convenient, but it is easy to forget that the promises end there:

  • no atomicity for compound operations: _count++ on a volatile field is still three steps, increments still get lost;
  • no write→read ordering: a release write and a following acquire read of another location can still swap.

The second one breaks "raise my flag, check the other flag" algorithms. You need a full fence: Interlocked or Thread.MemoryBarrier().
cards.deep:
volatile is not allowed on every type: references, pointers, integers up to 32 bits, bool, char, float, IntPtr/nint and enums based on them. On long and double you get error CS0677: on a 32-bit platform writing them is not atomic. Volatile.Read(ref long) does exist, and per the memory model spec it is atomic even on 32 bits.

The old Thread.VolatileRead/VolatileWrite from .NET Framework issued a full fence — they are slower and no longer needed: the Volatile class arrived in .NET Framework 4.5.

cards.q: In the code above both fields are volatile. Can you get r1 == 0 and r2 == 0?
options: Yes: volatile does not stop a read from overtaking an earlier write
Only on ARM64, never on x64
No, if the threads run on different cores
cards.explain: A release write holds back what came before it, an acquire read holds back what comes after it. The pair "write, then read" is covered by neither. On x64 it is exactly the one reordering the hardware does. A fence between the lines (Interlocked.Exchange instead of the write, or Thread.MemoryBarrier) rules this outcome out.

wrong.2: The opposite: write→read is exactly what x64 reorders by itself through the store buffer.

cards.title: What the .NET memory model guarantees
cards.body:
ECMA-335 promises little. The real runtime (CoreCLR) gives more, and it is written down in the memory model spec in dotnet/runtime:

  • aligned reads and writes up to pointer size are atomic — you never see half a value;
  • a volatile read is an acquire, a volatile write is a release;
  • storing an object reference to a shared location is a release: whoever reads the reference sees the object's fields initialized, without an extra fence;
  • ordering honors data dependency: a read through a reference does not happen before reading the reference itself;
  • Interlocked, Thread.MemoryBarrier and entering/leaving a lock are fences (Interlocked and MemoryBarrier are full ones).
cards.deep:
The cost differs by CPU. On x64 a volatile read or write is a plain mov: the hardware already gives acquire/release, the JIT just does not reorder or merge them. On ARM64 the JIT emits ldar/stlr (load-acquire / store-release) or a dmb barrier — the choice depends on the JIT version and the spot. A full fence on x64 is a lock instruction or mfence, on ARM64 it is dmb ish.

Note: the "storing a reference is a release" guarantee does not order two independent ordinary writes. If order matters, say so explicitly with Volatile.

cards.q: What is true about volatile in C#? Select all.
options: A long field cannot be declared volatile
_count++ on a volatile field becomes atomic
A read of a volatile field cannot be hoisted out of a loop
A volatile write and a following volatile read of another field can swap places
On x64 every volatile read is a separate fence instruction
cards.explain: long is forbidden (CS0677). ++ is still three steps — you need Interlocked. Hoisting is not allowed: every volatile read is real. The write→read pair is not ordered. On x64 a volatile read is a plain mov, the constraints apply to the JIT only.

cards.q: Match the operation with what it promises
pairs: Acquire: later operations will not move earlier
Release: earlier operations will not move later
A full fence in both directions
May be merged with a neighbor and hoisted out of a loop
Storing a reference to a new object
The reader sees the fields initialized

lessons.title: Interlocked and the CAS loop
lessons.sub: Atomic instructions, CompareExchange and lock-free updates

cards.title: What happens inside the CPU
cards.body:
You have already met Interlocked.Increment. Now — how it works. The JIT turns the call not into a method call but straight into an atomic instruction:

  • x64 — a lock-prefixed instruction: lock xadd for Add/Increment (or lock add when the result is unused), lock cmpxchg for CompareExchange, xchg for Exchange;
  • ARM64 — LSE atomic instructions (ldaddal, casal) if the CPU supports them, otherwise a loop of "exclusive load — conditional store".

The core takes the cache line into exclusive ownership, does the read-modify-write, and nobody can squeeze in between. It is also a full fence: no operation jumps over it in either direction.

cards.title: Cost: cheap until it gets crowded
cards.body:
Without contention an atomic operation costs on the order of a few to tens of nanoseconds — more than a plain ++, but far less than a trip into the kernel.

Under contention the picture changes. To write, a core needs the line in exclusive ownership. Sixteen threads hammering one counter make the line bounce between the cores' caches. Every operation waits until the line is handed over. Add threads — it gets slower.

The cure is the same as for false sharing: give each thread its own counter (or a ThreadLocal) and sum at the end.

cards.q: 16 threads call Interlocked.Increment on one field in a loop. Why is it slower than a single thread?
options: The cache line holding the counter bounces between cores, every operation waits for it
Interlocked takes a lock on an object, threads queue up
Under contention Interlocked falls back to the OS kernel
cards.explain: The atomic instruction blocks nothing and never enters the kernel. It simply cannot start until the core gets the line in exclusive ownership. The bottleneck is the cache coherence protocol.

wrong.1: There is no object and no Monitor here: it is a single CPU instruction.
wrong.3: Retries belong to the CAS loop you write yourself. Increment on x64 is a single atomic instruction, and it always succeeds.

cards.title: What Interlocked methods return
cards.body:
A common mistake is mixing up what comes back: the new value or the old one.

  • Increment, Decrement, Add — the new value;
  • Exchange — the old one: you write yours and get what was there;
  • CompareExchange — the old one, always, whether the swap happened or not;
  • And, Or (.NET 5+) — the old one;
  • Read(ref long) — an atomic read of a 64-bit number.
cards.code:
int n = 5;
Interlocked.Add(ref n, 3);        // returns 8
Interlocked.Exchange(ref n, 0);   // returns 8, n == 0
Interlocked.Or(ref n, 0b100);     // returns 0, n == 4
cards.deep:
Interlocked.Read exists only for long/ulong: in a 32-bit process a 64-bit read is two instructions, and without it you can read a "torn" value — the old half and the new half. In a 64-bit process an aligned long read is atomic anyway.

The set of overloads keeps growing: in .NET 9 Exchange and CompareExchange got versions for byte and short. For reference types there are the generic Exchange<T> and CompareExchange<T>.

cards.q: Match the call (n was 10) with what it returns

cards.title: CompareExchange — the brick of lock-free code
cards.body:
CompareExchange(ref location, value, comparand) atomically does: "if location holds comparand, write value". It returns what was in location before the call. This is CAS — compare-and-swap.

How to tell the swap succeeded: you got back exactly what you expected (comparand).

The trap is argument order: the new value first, then the expected one. Other languages and algorithm write-ups often do it the other way round.

cards.title: The CAS loop: read, compute, try
cards.body:
Interlocked can add, but it cannot "write the maximum". Any such update follows one pattern:

  • read the current value;
  • compute the new value from the old one;
  • CAS: write the new value if the old one has not changed;
  • failed — someone got there first; take what they wrote and repeat.

No lock, nobody sleeps. A thread that loses the race just redoes the computation with fresh data.

cards.q: Put the steps of one CAS loop iteration in order
items: Read the current value
Compute the new value from what you read
Call CompareExchange with what you read as the comparand
Compare the result with what you read
Not equal — take the returned value and repeat
cards.explain: The key is step 4: CompareExchange returns what was actually there. Equal to the expected value — the write went through. Not equal — that is your fresh value, no need to re-read the field.

cards.q: A lock-free stack. Under contention it loses items. Which line should be inside the loop but is outside?
cards.explain: After a lost attempt head is updated, but node.Next still points at the old top. The next CAS successfully puts node on top — and the chain skips the items other threads pushed in between. The node's link must be recomputed on every iteration: the "compute the new value" step belongs inside the loop.

cards.title: Lock-free does not mean wait-free
cards.body:
A CAS loop is lock-free: at any moment at least one thread makes progress, and a stalled thread holds nobody up. But it is not wait-free: a particular thread under heavy contention can lose again and again.

Rules for a CAS loop:

  • the computation inside is short and free of side effects: it may run several times;
  • CAS cannot update several fields at once — pack them into an immutable object and swap the reference;
  • immutable collections already have a ready-made loop: ImmutableInterlocked.Update.

If the logic is more than a couple of lines, a lock is simpler, and without contention it is almost as fast.
cards.deep: The ABA problem: CAS compares values, not history. It was A, became B, then A again — CAS decides nothing changed. In C/C++ this breaks lock-free stacks: a node is freed and reallocated at the same address. In .NET the garbage collector does not reuse an object's memory while a reference to it exists — and you hold one in head. So classic ABA with references does not happen here (unless you reuse nodes yourself through a pool), but with integers (counters, indices, versions) it remains.

cards.q: Lazy initialization without a lock: several threads may run the factory, but there will be one winner
cards.explain: We store our object only if the field still holds null. Got null back — we won, return created. Got non-null — someone was first, return their object, and ours becomes garbage. Exchange would overwrite another thread's object, and different threads would end up with different Config instances.

cards.q: What is true? Select all.
options: Every Interlocked method is a full memory fence
CompareExchange returns true if the swap succeeded
The body of a CAS loop may run several times
Under contention Interlocked.Increment puts the thread to sleep in the kernel
Interlocked.Read is needed for long in a 32-bit process
cards.explain: CompareExchange returns the old value, not a bool. Increment never enters the kernel — it waits for the cache line at the hardware level. The loop body repeats on every lost attempt, so it must have no side effects.

lessons.title: Spin or sleep
lessons.sub: SpinWait and SpinLock vs Mutex, Semaphore and kernel events

cards.title: Two ways to wait
cards.body:
The lock is taken. What should a thread do?

  • Spin: check in a loop whether it was released. The thread stays in user mode, keeps its quantum and reacts within nanoseconds. But all that time it burns a CPU core for nothing.
  • Sleep in the OS kernel: ask the scheduler to take the thread off the CPU and wake it on a signal. The core is free for others. But the switch to kernel mode and back, the context switch and the wake-up cost a few microseconds, and the woken thread still waits for its turn.

Hence the rule: spinning pays off only if the wait will be shorter than the cost of falling asleep and waking up, and there is a second core on which the lock owner is running right now.

cards.q: When is pure spinning worse than sleeping in the kernel?
options: The lock owner was preempted and is not running: the waiter burns its quantum until it comes back
The lock is held for 50 nanoseconds on a 16-core machine
The critical section is a single assignment
cards.explain: While the owner is not running, nobody can release the lock — spinning is guaranteed to be useless. On a single core it is the worst case: the spinning thread itself keeps the owner from getting the CPU. The other options are exactly the good cases for spinning.

cards.title: SpinWait: a spin that knows when to stop
cards.body:
Writing while (!flag) { } by hand is bad: endless starvation on one core, extra heat and interference with the sibling hyperthread on many. The SpinWait struct does it right:

  • the first SpinOnce() calls really spin, with a hint instruction to the CPU (pause on x64) and a growing iteration count;
  • after about ten calls it starts yielding the CPU: Thread.Yield, Sleep(0), sometimes Sleep(1);
  • on a single-core machine it yields right away.

NextSpinWillYield tells you it is time to switch to a real wait. A ready-made wrapper is SpinWait.SpinUntil(condition, timeout).

cards.title: SpinLock — a struct with sharp edges
cards.body:
SpinLock is a lock that spins under contention using that same SpinWait. It allocates no objects and never touches the kernel, so it suits critical sections of a few instructions that are taken very often.

The sharp edges:

  • it is a struct: a copy is a separate lock. Do not pass it by value and do not keep it in a readonly field;
  • it is not reentrant: re-entering on the same thread throws LockRecursionException with owner tracking, and spins forever without it;
  • the Enter(ref bool lockTaken) signature is the same as Monitor's, for a reliable finally.

Rule: start with lock. Move to SpinLock only if the profiler showed that this particular lock is hot.

cards.q: Under load items get lost, even though every write is under the SpinLock. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: Calling a method on a struct in a readonly field works on a defensive copy: each Enter takes its own temporary lock, and there is no mutual exclusion. Remove readonly — then Enter changes the field itself.

cards.title: Kernel objects: WaitHandle
cards.body:
Mutex, Semaphore, EventWaitHandle (and its children AutoResetEvent, ManualResetEvent) wrap OS objects. All of them derive from WaitHandle and hold a kernel handle.

  • The cost: on Windows every WaitOne, Set, Release is a system call, even when there was nothing to wait for. On Linux and macOS the runtime emulates these objects in its own layer, with no system call on a free object, but the path is still long. Either way it is tens of times more expensive than entering a free lock.
  • The strength: an object can have a name, and then other processes see it. Plus WaitHandle.WaitAny/WaitAll — wait on several objects at once.

Cross-process synchronization is the main reason to use them today. Inside one process there is almost always a lightweight replacement: lock, SemaphoreSlim, ManualResetEventSlim.
cards.deep:
Names behave differently. On Windows all three types can be named; the Global\ prefix makes a name visible across all sessions, Local\ (the default) only within your own. On Linux and macOS the runtime emulates only the named Mutex; a name on a Semaphore or EventWaitHandle there leads to PlatformNotSupportedException.

In .NET Framework WaitHandle derived from MarshalByRefObject and also served to synchronize across AppDomains. Modern .NET has no application domains.

cards.q: Match the primitive with its trait
pairs: Tied to the owning thread, can be cross-process
A counter in the kernel, any thread may release it
Set lets one waiter through and closes
After Set it is open for everyone until Reset
A struct, waits in user mode

cards.title: Mutex: the owner and the abandoned lock
cards.body:
A Mutex remembers its owning thread. Only the thread that took it may release it: ReleaseMutex from another thread throws ApplicationException. So, as with lock, an await between acquire and release is a bug.

It is reentrant: the owner may take it again, but must release it the same number of times.

If the owning thread or process died without releasing the mutex, the OS hands it to the next waiter, who gets an AbandonedMutexException. The lock is already theirs, but the data under it may be half-modified.

The classic use is "only one instance of the program":

cards.q: Prevent a second instance of the program from starting
cards.explain: You need an object other processes can see — a named Mutex. The last parameter tells whether we created it (the first instance) or opened an existing one. SemaphoreSlim and Monitor live only inside one process.

cards.q: Three threads wait in WaitOne() on one AutoResetEvent. Another thread calls Set() once. What happens?
options: One thread wakes up, the event closes again
One wakes up, the event stays open
None: Set has no effect without Reset
cards.explain: AutoResetEvent is a turnstile: one pass per Set. ManualResetEvent is a gate: after Set everyone passes until someone calls Reset.

cards.q: What is true? Select all.
options: On Windows every WaitOne on a Mutex is a system call, even if the mutex is free
A Semaphore can be released from another thread
SpinWait on a single-core machine yields the CPU right away
A named Semaphore works on Linux the same way as on Windows
cards.explain: SpinLock is not reentrant — unlike Monitor and Mutex. On Linux and macOS only mutexes can be named; for Semaphore and EventWaitHandle names are supported on Windows only.

lessons.title: Hybrid locks
lessons.sub: Monitor inside out, Wait/Pulse, the Lock type in .NET 9 and the Slim family

cards.title: The best of spinning and of the kernel
cards.body:
Pure spinning burns the CPU, a kernel object is expensive even without contention. A hybrid lock takes the best of both and goes through three stages:

  • the fast path: the lock is free — one atomic CompareExchange and you are in. No kernel, no allocations, tens of nanoseconds;
  • a short spin: the lock is taken — spin a little, maybe the owner is about to leave;
  • sleep: did not make it — sleep on a kernel object until the owner wakes you on exit.

That is how lock (Monitor), the new Lock, SemaphoreSlim, ManualResetEventSlim and ReaderWriterLockSlim work. The Slim suffix means exactly this: a lightweight hybrid version with no kernel handle on the fast path.

cards.title: Monitor inside out
cards.body:
Where does lock (obj) keep its state? In the object header — the word in front of the type pointer. While there is no contention it holds a "thin lock": the owner thread's id and a recursion count. Taking it is one CAS on the header.

When a second thread finds the lock taken, it spins a little. If that does not help, the lock inflates: the CLR creates a sync block for the object — an entry in a separate table with a queue of waiters and a kernel event to sleep on. The sync block index is written into the header.

The compiler expands the statement itself like this (since C# 4):
cards.deep:
The header is small, and the thin lock shares it with the default hash code. If the non-overridden GetHashCode was already called on the object, the hash sits in the header and lock goes straight through a sync block — and vice versa. That is why sync blocks exist at all: they hold whatever did not fit — the hash, the lock, COM interop data.

A sync block lives as long as the object. Hence the advice to lock on a dedicated private object: foreign code that does lock on your this or on typeof(...) shares the very same lock with you.

cards.q: Why does Monitor.Enter take a ref bool lockTaken parameter, when people used to write just Monitor.Enter(obj) before try?
options: An exception could hit between taking the lock and entering try, and the lock would stay taken forever
So that Enter can return false on a timeout
So that the JIT does not hoist Enter out of a loop
cards.explain: In .NET Framework an asynchronous exception (ThreadAbortException) could arrive between Enter and try. The lock is taken, and finally never runs. With lockTaken, Enter itself is inside try, and finally knows for sure whether to release. TryEnter is for timeouts, and Monitor is reentrant anyway.

cards.title: Wait and Pulse: waiting for a condition under a lock
cards.body:
Monitor is not just a lock but also a condition variable. A thread under the lock sees it is too early to continue (the queue is empty) and calls Monitor.Wait. That atomically releases the lock and puts the thread to sleep in the object's waiting queue.

Another thread takes the lock, changes the state and calls Pulse — moving one waiter to the ready queue (PulseAll moves all). The woken thread re-acquires the lock and only then returns from Wait.

Both methods may be called only while holding the lock on that object, otherwise you get SynchronizationLockException.

cards.q: Put the events in order: a consumer waits, a producer adds an item
items: The consumer takes the lock and sees an empty queue
Wait releases the lock, the consumer falls asleep
The producer takes the lock and adds an item
Pulse moves the consumer to the ready queue
The producer leaves the lock
The consumer re-acquires the lock and re-checks the condition
cards.explain: Pulse does not hand over the lock by itself: the consumer really wakes only when the producer leaves the lock. And between these moments a third thread can grab the lock.

cards.q: Two consumers. Sometimes Dequeue throws InvalidOperationException: the queue is empty. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: Between Pulse and re-acquiring the lock, the second consumer can walk into the lock "from the street" and take the item. The first one wakes up, no longer checks the condition and reaches into an empty queue. The condition after Wait is always re-checked in a while loop.

cards.title: The Lock type in .NET 9
cards.body:
Since .NET 9 and C# 13 there is a dedicated System.Threading.Lock type. The lock state lives in the fields of the Lock object itself, not in the header of an arbitrary object and not in the sync block table. The docs recommend it for new locks as the fastest option.

The compiler recognizes the type: lock on a Lock becomes not Monitor.Enter but using (_gate.EnterScope()). EnterScope returns a ref struct whose Dispose releases the lock.

The catch: cast the Lock to object — and lock silently becomes the old header-based Monitor. The compiler warns: CS9216. And Lock has no Wait/Pulse: for condition variables you still need Monitor.

cards.q: Write what the C# 13 compiler turns a lock on the new type into
cards.explain: EnterScope takes the lock and returns a Scope struct, and using guarantees its Dispose — leaving the lock — even on an exception. With a field of type object the compiler would generate Monitor.Enter/Exit.

cards.title: The Slim family and ReaderWriterLockSlim
cards.body:
• SemaphoreSlim — a user-mode counter. You know the main thing from the pitfalls unit: it has WaitAsync, and it is not tied to a thread.
  • ManualResetEventSlim — spins first, then waits through Monitor. It creates a real kernel event only if you ask for the WaitHandle property.
  • ReaderWriterLockSlim — many readers or one writer. There is an "upgradeable read" mode: you read and, if needed, upgrade the lock to a write. While a writer is waiting, new readers are held back — so the writer does not starve.

ReaderWriterLockSlim has its own cost for all that: tracking readers is more expensive than a plain lock. It wins only when reads vastly outnumber writes and each read takes noticeably longer than entering the lock.
cards.deep:
By default ReaderWriterLockSlim is created with LockRecursionPolicy.NoRecursion: re-entering on the same thread throws LockRecursionException. Only one thread at a time may hold an upgradeable read — otherwise two "upgrading" readers would wait for each other. The object is IDisposable.

The old ReaderWriterLock from .NET Framework 1.x is slower and has known problems — new code does not need it. All Slim primitives, like Monitor, work only inside one process.

cards.q: A reference data cache: 99% of calls are a 100 ns dictionary lookup, reloads are rare. What does replacing lock with ReaderWriterLockSlim give you?
options: Most likely nothing, or a slowdown: tracking readers costs about as much as the read itself
A speedup by the number of cores: readers do not get in each other's way
A deadlock on the first reload
Nothing changes: inside it is the same Monitor
cards.explain: Every reader entry is atomic operations on a shared counter, and its cache line bounces between cores just like with lock. With short reads there is no gain. Better here is an immutable snapshot of the data: readers take the reference without a lock, a reload swaps it via Volatile.Write or Interlocked.Exchange.

cards.q: Match the task with the primitive
pairs: lock on a field of type Lock
Wait for a condition under a lock
One thread opens the gate for many

cards.q: What is true? Select all.
options: A free lock is taken without entering the kernel
Monitor.Wait can be called without holding the lock on that object
A Lock cast to object behaves like Monitor in a lock statement
SemaphoreSlim can be released from another thread
cards.explain: Wait without the lock throws SynchronizationLockException. Lock is mutual exclusion only, it has no condition variables. Casting to object throws away the whole point of the new type — that is what warning CS9216 is about.

lessons.title: Lazy and concurrent collections
lessons.sub: Double-checked locking, Lazy<T> modes, ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd

cards.title: Double-checked locking
cards.body:
The object is expensive, it must be created once, and it is read all the time. Taking a lock on every read feels wasteful. Hence double-checked locking:

  • the first check is without a lock: the object exists — return it right away;
  • it does not — take the lock and check again: while we waited for the lock, another thread may have created the object.

Does this work without volatile? Under the general ECMA spec — no. In CoreCLR — yes: storing an object reference is a release, and a read through a reference honors data dependency (lesson 1). But only if the object is fully ready before the reference is written to the field.
cards.deep: For a singleton you usually need no double check at all. static readonly Settings Instance = Settings.Load(); — and the CLR itself guarantees the type initializer runs exactly once, under its own internal lock. The price is less control over when creation happens: without a static constructor the type is marked beforefieldinit, and initialization may happen before the first access.

cards.q: Another thread sometimes gets Settings with empty fields. Which line lets the object out before it is ready?
cards.explain: After this line the field is no longer null, and the first check in another thread lets it past the lock — to an object that is not loaded yet. Create and set up the object in a local variable, and write it to the field as the very last step.

cards.title: Lazy<T>: double-checked locking written for you
cards.body:
Lazy<T> stores a factory and calls it on the first access to Value. How it behaves under contention is set by LazyThreadSafetyMode:

  • ExecutionAndPublication (the default) — the factory runs under a lock, exactly once, other threads wait for the result;
  • PublicationOnly — no lock: several threads may run the factory at the same time, the first finished result lands in the field (via CompareExchange), the rest are thrown away;
  • None — no synchronization, for single-threaded objects. The fastest.

cards.q: Match the lazy initialization option with its behavior
pairs: Factory under a lock, exactly one run
The factory may run several times, the first result wins
No Lazy object: a field and CompareExchange

cards.title: Exceptions in the factory and LazyInitializer
cards.body:
A non-obvious behavior: if the factory throws in ExecutionAndPublication mode (or None), Lazy remembers the exception. Every later access to Value throws the same exception, and the factory is never called again. A network glitch at startup — and the object is "broken" until restart.

In PublicationOnly mode exceptions are not cached: the next access tries again.

If you do not want a separate Lazy object per field, there is LazyInitializer.EnsureInitialized(ref field, factory). Without an explicit lock it behaves like PublicationOnly: it checks the field for null and publishes the result via CompareExchange — just like the code from the Interlocked lesson.

cards.q: A Lazy<HttpConfig> in the default mode. On the first Value the factory threw HttpRequestException: the network was down. A minute later the network is up. What does the next Value access give?
options: The same HttpRequestException: the exception is cached
The factory runs again and returns the config
InvalidOperationException: the Lazy is in a faulted state
cards.explain: ExecutionAndPublication caches the factory exception forever. If the failure can be transient — use PublicationOnly, your own retry code, or recreate the Lazy.

wrong.1: Only PublicationOnly behaves like that. The default mode remembers the exception.

cards.title: ConcurrentDictionary inside out
cards.body:
ConcurrentDictionary is not a regular dictionary under a single lock.

  • Reads (TryGetValue, the indexer) take no locks: buckets are published so that a reader always sees a consistent state.
  • Writes take only the lock of their stripe (striped locking): an array of locks, each covering part of the buckets. Writers in different stripes do not interfere.
  • Operations over the whole dictionary — Count, Keys, Values, ToArray — take all locks at once. Calling them in a hot loop means stopping every writer.
  • A foreach is safe during concurrent changes, but it is not a snapshot: you may see some of the changes made during the enumeration.

cards.title: GetOrAdd and a factory that runs several times
cards.body:
GetOrAdd(key, factory) looks atomic, but the dictionary calls the factory outside the lock — so that slow or reentrant foreign code does not hold a stripe. Therefore:

  • several threads that miss the key at the same time will all run the factory;
  • one value ends up in the dictionary, and everyone gets exactly that one;
  • the other created values are simply thrown away — without Dispose.

For a cheap factory it does not matter. For an expensive one or one with side effects (a connection, a file, a paid request) you store not the value but a Lazy<T>. Extra Lazy objects cost next to nothing, and the factory inside the winning one runs once.
cards.deep: Same with AddOrUpdate: the dictionary also calls the update function outside the lock and repeats it on a race — it is a CAS loop over the value. So it must not contain side effects. There are GetOrAdd<TArg>(key, factory, arg) overloads: the argument is passed explicitly, the lambda captures nothing — no closure allocation per call.

cards.q: 10 threads call GetOrAdd with the same new key at the same time. What is true?
options: The factory may run 1 to 10 times, but all threads get the same value
The factory runs exactly once: GetOrAdd is atomic
Each thread gets its own value, the dictionary keeps the last one
Nine threads get an exception: the key was already added
cards.explain: The factory is outside the lock, so its runs are not limited. The insertion is under the stripe lock: the first insertion wins, the other threads see the key on the re-check and return the winner's value.

cards.q: Make the expensive connection open only once per key
cards.explain: Several threads may each create a Lazy object, but only one ends up in the dictionary, and everyone calls Value on it. The default ExecutionAndPublication mode guarantees a single Connection.Open. Remember the exception cache: a failed open stays in the dictionary — remove it with TryRemove.

cards.title: The other collections and the check-then-act trap
cards.body:
• ConcurrentQueue — no locks on the common path, array segments; the best choice for FIFO between threads.
  • ConcurrentStack — a linked list on a CAS loop, like the stack from the Interlocked lesson.
  • ConcurrentBag — each thread has its own list; it pays off when the same thread both adds and takes. As a general-purpose queue it is slower than ConcurrentQueue.
  • BlockingCollection — a blocking wrapper with a bounded capacity. In async code Channel replaces it.

The main trap: each operation is thread-safe, but their combination is not. if (!d.ContainsKey(k)) d[k] = v; — another thread gets in between the check and the write. You need one operation: TryAdd, GetOrAdd, AddOrUpdate, TryRemove, TryUpdate.

cards.q: What is true? Select all.
options: Reading from a ConcurrentDictionary takes no locks
Count on a ConcurrentDictionary is cheap: it reads one field
Lazy in the default mode remembers the factory exception
The GetOrAdd factory is called under the stripe lock
ContainsKey followed by the indexer is not atomic, even on a ConcurrentDictionary
cards.explain: Count takes all the dictionary locks. The dictionary calls the GetOrAdd factory outside the lock on purpose, so it may run several times. Only a single operation is atomic, not a sequence of them.

lessons.title: Course final
lessons.sub: From memory fences to async locks

cards.q: A background thread spins while (!_stop) { … } on a plain bool field. In Release it sometimes does not stop after _stop = true. Which fix is reliable?
options: Add Thread.Sleep(0) to the loop body
Wrap only the _stop = true write in a lock
cards.explain: The JIT may read a plain field once and hoist the read out of the loop. Volatile.Read (or volatile on the field) forbids that. A call inside the loop merely gets in the way of one particular optimization and guarantees nothing, and a lock on one side only does not order the reads on the other.

cards.q: Code ran for years on x64 servers and started breaking after moving to ARM64. What could have shown up for the first time? Select all.
options: Two plain writes became visible to another core in reverse order
Two plain reads of different fields executed in reverse order
An aligned int write stopped being atomic
Interlocked.CompareExchange stopped being a full fence
cards.explain: x64 reorders only write→read, ARM64 reorders all four pairs. Atomicity of aligned writes up to pointer size and the full fence of Interlocked are guaranteed on both architectures.

cards.q: Add returns right away, but the total does not change. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: The arguments are swapped: the new value comes first, then the expected one. Here the CAS expects current + amount in the field, which is not there — nothing is written, current is returned, and the method thinks it succeeded. Correct: CompareExchange(ref _total, current + amount, current).

cards.q: Put in order the path of a thread that hit a taken lock
items: Try to take the lock with one CAS
Spin briefly in user mode
Sleep on a kernel object
The owner leaves the lock and wakes a waiter
The woken thread tries to take the lock again
cards.explain: All hybrid locks work this way: a fast path without the kernel, a little spinning, and only then an expensive sleep. A woken thread does not get the lock automatically — it competes for it again.

cards.q: Which line will not compile?
cards.explain: CS1996: await inside a lock body is forbidden — both with Monitor and with the new Lock. The lock belongs to a thread, and after await the method may continue on another one. The async lock is SemaphoreSlim with WaitAsync and Release in finally.

cards.q: Which primitives can be released from another thread, and so survive an await between acquire and release? Select all.
cards.explain: Semaphores have no owner — only a counter. Monitor, Mutex and Lock remember the owning thread and are released only by it. But only SemaphoreSlim fits async code: Semaphore has no WaitAsync, its WaitOne blocks the thread.

cards.q: Match the task with the tool
pairs: A request counter from many threads
One instance of the program per machine
A critical section with await inside
An expensive per-key factory in a cache
Producer and consumer in async code

cards.q: WPF, a button handler calls LoadAsync().Result, and LoadAsync contains an await without ConfigureAwait(false). The window froze forever. Why?
options: The continuation after await waits for the UI thread, and the UI thread is blocked in .Result waiting for the continuation
The thread pool is exhausted, and the continuation has nowhere to run
.Result threw an AggregateException, and the window stopped processing messages
A Task created on the UI thread cannot be awaited from the UI thread
cards.explain: The classic synchronization context deadlock: two parties wait for each other, like two threads taking locks in opposite order. The cure is async all the way up; ConfigureAwait(false) in a library is the second line of defense.

cards.q: Which order of picking a synchronization tool makes sense?
options: Ready-made high-level tools (Channel, Concurrent collections, Lazy), then lock, and only after measuring — Interlocked and volatile
volatile on every shared field first: it is the cheapest way, everything else only when needed
A named Mutex wherever there is shared data: it works even across processes
SpinLock instead of lock throughout the code: it never enters the kernel and so is always faster
cards.explain: The lower the level, the more ways to get it wrong: volatile does not make ++ atomic, a CAS loop is easy to get backwards, SpinLock breaks when copied. High-level tools are already debugged, and an uncontended lock costs tens of nanoseconds.
